docs.title: RayON
docs.text: A CUDA & OptiX path tracer with real-time progressive sampling, volumetric clouds and ray-marched shapes

docs.title: What is RayON?
docs.text:
RayON is an educational and experimental path tracer written in C++17 and CUDA. It started as a re-implementation of the classic Ray Tracing in One Weekend series and grew into an interactive renderer that holds 60 frames per second while the camera moves and accumulates thousands of samples per pixel when it stops. It is used as teaching material in the ISC 302 High-Performance Computing course at HES-SO Valais.

Two GPU back-ends share one scene description and one GUI, each in an offline and an interactive flavour. No recompilation is needed to switch between them (-m 2 to -m 5):

OptiX (hardware ray tracing)

Triangles on the RT cores, custom intersectors for spheres, rectangles and SDF shapes, an AI denoiser for motion frames and a regulator that trades resolution for frame rate. The default when the OptiX SDK is found.

CUDA (software ray tracing)

One thread per pixel, a BVH traversed with an iterative stack, persistent random states and a float accumulation buffer that never leaves the GPU. Runs everywhere CUDA runs.

Interactive mode

SDL2 window with mouse orbit, pan and zoom, a Dear ImGui panel for every rendering parameter, scene switching with the arrow keys, HDR skies, and a button that writes the camera and the light settings back into the scene file.

CPU renderers archived

The original CPU rendering back-ends (sequential and multi-threaded) live on the legacy/cpu-renderer branch. The main branch is GPU only.

docs.title: What it renders
docs.text:
• Materials: Lambertian, mirror, rough mirror, glass, GGX anisotropic conductors with measured complex IOR, thin-film interference, clear coat, area and sphere lights, and a volume material for clouds and smoke (delta tracking, Henyey–Greenstein phase function, volumetric shadow rays).
  • Geometry: spheres, rectangles, triangles, Wavefront OBJ meshes with MTL materials and UV textures, procedurally displaced spheres, ten ray-marched signed distance primitives, and volumes shaped by a mesh, by procedural noise or by an OpenVDB density grid.
  • Light transport: next event estimation with multiple importance sampling, a Sobol' low-discrepancy sampler with Owen scrambling, Russian roulette, adaptive (converged-pixel) sampling, a BVH built with the surface area heuristic.
  • Scenes: a plain YAML format with 24 bundled examples, from a Cornell box to the Stanford bunny as a cumulus cloud.

docs.title: Sample renders
docs.text: Cloud bunny — the volume material: a mesh shaped by noise, lit by a sun with volumetric shadow rays. Scene 17_cloud_bunny.yaml. VDB bunny — the same transport on a density grid from OpenVDB, the reference image of the pbrt book. Scene 19_vdb_bunny.yaml. SDF gallery — mandelbulb, death star, cut hollow sphere, torus, octahedron, pyramid and friends, sphere-traced on both back-ends. Scene 18_sdf_shapes.yaml. Cornell box — diffuse colour bleeding and soft shadows from a rectangular area light, resolved by next event estimation. Anisotropic metals and glass — GGX microfacet conductors with measured spectral Fresnel next to dielectrics. Thin film — soap bubbles and oil slicks from the Airy interference formula.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
# Build (CMake ≥ 3.20, a C++17 compiler, the CUDA toolkit; SDL2 and the OptiX SDK are optional)
mkdir -p build && cd build
cmake .. --fresh
make -j$(nproc)

# Run from build/ — the OptiX programs and the HDR skies are found relative to this directory.
# Interactive OptiX when available, else interactive CUDA, else offline CUDA.
./rayon

# Pick a mode explicitly: 2 = CUDA offline, 3 = CUDA interactive, 4 = OptiX offline, 5 = OptiX interactive
./rayon -m 4 -s 512 -r 1080 --scene ../resources/scenes/17_cloud_bunny.yaml

See Getting Started for the full setup, the command-line options and the list of bundled scenes, or YAML Scene Format to write your own.

docs.title: About the RayON project
docs.text:
RayON started as a clean-room reimplementation of the Ray Tracing in One Weekend series — a personal exercise to understand the mechanics of stochastic light transport from first principles. It grew into a full-featured interactive GPU path tracer used as an educational resource in the CS302 High-Performance Computing course for the ISC bachelor programme at HES-SO Valais.

The project demonstrates:

  • How one scene description drives two GPU back-ends, a software path tracer in CUDA and a hardware-accelerated one on OptiX, without duplicating the scene logic.
  • Progressive sample accumulation and interactive camera control at real-time frame rates, with a regulator that trades resolution for frame rate while the camera moves.
  • Physically-based materials, from Lambertian and microfacet conductors to thin films, clear coats and participating media, with next event estimation and multiple importance sampling.
  • Ray-marched signed distance shapes and volumetric clouds from procedural noise or OpenVDB data.

The source code is published under the GPL v3 licence and is intended as a learning resource as much as a working renderer.

docs.title: About the author
docs.text:
Pierre-André Mudry is head of Computer Science and Communication degree programme and a professor at the University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland (HES-SO Valais-Wallis) in Sion, where he teaches and conducts research in the Systems Engineering department.

His work sits at the intersection of embedded systems, digital hardware design, and applied machine learning. He has a particular interest in bridging the gap between algorithm and silicon — from high-level language design for constrained devices through to FPGA implementation and IoT deployment. Recent work has explored edge inference, non-invasive flow metering with neural networks, and anomaly detection on resource-limited hardware.

docs.title: Gallery
docs.text:
Renders from the bundled scenes, grouped by what they show. Every image can be reproduced from resources/scenes/ with the offline modes (-m 4 or -m 2).

Volumes & SDFScenesMaterialsVisualisation & DebugProgressive QualityHDR Skies

Cloud bunny — 17_cloud_bunny.yaml. The volume material with procedural shape noise, a hidden sun and volumetric shadow rays. OptiX, 512 spp, 720p. VDB bunny — 19_vdb_bunny.yaml. The OpenVDB bunny_cloud grid, 289×286×219 cells, read straight into the 3D density texture. OptiX, 512 spp, 720p. VDB bunny, 2048 spp, 1080p — the same scene left to converge. SDF gallery — 18_sdf_shapes.yaml. Mandelbulb, death star, cut hollow sphere, torus, glass octahedron, pyramid, capsule, box, cylinder and sphere, sphere-traced on the GPU. OptiX, 384 spp, 720p.

Cornell box — 09_color_bleed_box.yaml. Coloured diffuse walls bleed onto the neighbouring surfaces; the area light overhead gives soft shadows. Indoor spheres — dielectric, metallic and diffuse spheres in an enclosed room with area lighting. ISC spheres — the five colours of the ISC programme's majors, with strong inter-reflections between specular surfaces. BVH test scene — 01_bvh_test_scene.yaml, 150 spheres used to measure the acceleration structure. Golf ball — a displaced sphere: the dimple pattern is procedural, and its count, radius and depth are live sliders in the GUI. Anisotropic metals — 01_anisotropic_metals_test.yaml at 512 spp: anisotropy along the rows, roughness along the columns.

Tinted rough mirrors — gold, copper and steel tints. The roughness blurs the reflection, from a perfect mirror at 0 towards diffuse at 1. Dielectrics and metals — glass follows Snell's law with Schlick's Fresnel approximation; the caustic under the sphere emerges from the path tracing alone. Thin film — 11_soap_bubbles.yaml. The Airy interference formula at several film thicknesses sweeps through the spectrum. Clear coat — a Lambertian base under a smooth dielectric coat; the highlight is view-dependent. UV texture mapping — 13_texture_test1.yaml. A grid texture through MTL files, interpolated with barycentric coordinates. MTL-driven textures — 14_texture_test2.yaml. Each group of a Blender export picks its texture from the .mtl file.

Normals — key N maps the surface normal to RGB (R = X, G = Y, B = Z). The smooth interpolation hides the face boundaries of the mesh. Interactive mode — the SDL2 window with the Dear ImGui panel: sample counter, convergence and the live sliders. OBJ loading — an imported mesh rendered with the vertex normals of the file. Depth of field — thin-lens aperture and focus distance, adjustable live in the Camera Settings section.

The anisotropic metals scene at increasing sample counts. Monte Carlo noise decays as \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N})\): every doubling of the samples removes about 30 % of the noise. The anisotropic highlights are the slowest to resolve.

4 spp — the highlights are buried in noise. 16 spp — shapes emerge, the streaks are faintly visible. 32 spp — the anisotropic streaks form. 64 spp — usable; the direction of the highlights is clear on the smooth spheres. 128 spp — clean for most materials. 512 spp — near convergence.

Scenes lit by equirectangular HDR environments from Poly Haven (CC0). Six environments are downloaded by bash resources/hdri/download_hdri.sh 8k, see HDR Sky Dome.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page walks you through building RayON from source, running your first render, and the command-line options.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Dependency Version Required? Notes C++ compiler C++17 Yes Clang (default, USE_CLANG=ON) or GCC CMake ≥ 3.20 Yes Generates compile_commands.json for clangd CUDA Toolkit ≥ 12.0 Yes Both back-ends are CUDA programs; the architecture is set to native NVIDIA OptiX SDK 8.0 or 9.0 Optional Enables modes 4 and 5 (hardware ray tracing). Found through OptiX_INSTALL_DIR, ~/Downloads/NVIDIA-OptiX-SDK-*, /usr/local/NVIDIA-OptiX-SDK or /opt/optix SDL2 ≥ 2.0 Optional Enables the interactive modes 3 and 5 Dear ImGui, stb bundled — Included under src/external/

Without SDL2 the offline modes still work. Without the OptiX SDK only the CUDA back-end is built.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/pmudry/RayON.git
cd RayON

mkdir -p build && cd build
cmake .. --fresh          # prints which of SDL2 and OptiX were found
make -j$(nproc)

VS Code users

Use the pre-defined tasks via Ctrl+Shift+P → Run Task: CMake: fresh, Make build and Launch. clangd picks up compile_commands.json and the .clangd file that CMake maintains with the include paths of every directory under src/.

docs.title: Build variants
docs.text:
cmake .. --fresh -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug      # -lineinfo for cuda-gdb and Nsight, no fast math
cmake .. --fresh -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release    # default: -O3 and --use_fast_math
cmake .. --fresh -DUSE_CLANG=OFF               # GCC instead of Clang for the host code
cmake .. --fresh -DENABLE_CLANG_TIDY=ON        # static analysis during the build (.clang-tidy)
cmake .. --fresh -DENABLE_DIAGS=ON             # extra diagnostic output in the renderers

After adding files or directories under src/, re-run cmake .. --fresh so the include paths and compile_commands.json are regenerated.

docs.title: Running RayON
docs.text:
Run from build/

The OptiX programs (optix_programs.ptx) and the HDR skies (../resources/hdri/) are located relative to the current directory. Every example below assumes cd build.

cd build
./rayon

With no -m the renderer picks the best mode it was built with: 5 (OptiX interactive) when both OptiX and SDL2 are available, else 4, else 3, else 2.

./rayon -m 2          # CUDA offline
./rayon -m 3          # CUDA interactive (SDL2)
./rayon -m 4          # OptiX offline
./rayon -m 5          # OptiX interactive (SDL2 + OptiX)
./rayon --menu        # ask which mode to use

Offline renders are written to build/rendered_images/ as a timestamped .png with a .json metadata file and a .txt log next to it; latest.png always holds the most recent image. The offline progress bar shows the elapsed time and an estimate of the time left.

docs.title: Command-line options
docs.text:
./rayon [options]
Flag Default Description -m <method> 5 (3 without OptiX) Renderer: 2 = CUDA offline, 3 = CUDA interactive, 4 = OptiX offline, 5 = OptiX interactive --menu — Show the mode selection menu instead of using the default --scene <yaml> built-in Load a scene from a YAML file -s <n> 64 Samples per pixel (offline modes 2, 4) -r <h> 720 Image height; the width follows the 16:9 aspect ratio (-r 1080) -r <WxH> — Arbitrary resolution (-r 1920x1080, -r 800x600) --sampler <sobol\|pcg> sobol GPU sampler: low-discrepancy Sobol' or classic PCG --no-hdr-cache off Always re-decode .hdr files instead of reading the .hdrcache sidecar --sky <name> gradient Interactive modes: start with this HDR sky of resources/hdri/ (part of the file name, e.g. --sky sunflowers) --samples-per-batch <n> 8 Interactive samples per batch; overrides the scene's settings.samples_per_batch --no-adaptive-sampling off Disable converged-pixel skipping --no-auto-accumulate off Do not keep adding samples while the camera is still --theme <name> nord GUI theme: light, classic, nord, dracula, gruvbox, catppuccin -h, --help — Print the help and exit

docs.title: MIS / NEE options (all modes)
docs.text:
Flag Default Description --no-mis MIS on Disable multiple importance sampling and next event estimation (faster per sample, much noisier) --motion-gate-mis off Disable MIS while the camera moves (interactive modes only) --nee-stride <N> 1 Beyond the first bounce, trace the shadow ray on 1 of every N samples and scale its contribution by N

The target frame rate while moving, the quality floors, the denoiser and the adaptive sampling threshold are GUI settings, see Interactive Mode.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# High-quality offline render with OptiX
./rayon -m 4 --scene ../resources/scenes/09_color_bleed_box.yaml -s 2048 -r 1080

# Fast preview with CUDA
./rayon -m 2 --scene ../resources/scenes/default_scene.yaml -s 8 -r 360

# Interactive session on the cloud bunny
./rayon --scene ../resources/scenes/17_cloud_bunny.yaml

# Interactive with a custom theme and no adaptive sampling
./rayon --theme dracula --no-adaptive-sampling

docs.title: Interactive mode on a remote GPU server
docs.text:
The SDL window does not work through ssh -X. Start a VNC session on the server instead:

sudo apt install tigervnc-standalone-server openbox   # once, on the server
scripts/rayon_vnc.sh -r 1080 --scene resources/scenes/18_sdf_shapes.yaml

The script starts a headless VNC server sized to the render resolution, runs rayon inside it and prints the vncviewer command to connect from your machine. Ctrl-C stops everything.

docs.title: Development History
docs.text:
CPU renderers archived

The CPU rendering backends discussed in the early milestones have been moved to the legacy/cpu-renderer branch. The main branch now supports GPU rendering only. Historical references below are preserved for context.

A walkthrough of how RayON grew from a 53-line main.cc into a multi-backend interactive GPU path tracer — told through the git history.

The project spans a bit more than a year, from a first "hello sphere" on a September evening to an OptiX renderer with volumetric clouds the following autumn, with long breaks in between. Each milestone below corresponds to a real commit (or small cluster of commits) and captures both what was built and why it mattered at that stage.

LLM usage across the project

Milestones 1–6 were written entirely by hand, with no LLM assistance. LLM tools were first introduced in Milestone 7 for specific features (SDF shapes, YAML loader, Cornell box). The last four milestones (12–15) were mainly implemented with LLM assistance, ranging from full implementation to collaborative design and partial coding. Individual milestones note where and how AI was involved. The October 2026 work (milestones 19 to 21) was implemented with Claude Code, with the author directing the design, testing every change in the GUI and deciding what to keep.

docs.title: Milestone 1 — The First Pixel (Sept 7–8, 2025)
docs.text:
Commit: 7901473 → b6af112

The repository starts with a CMakeLists, a .gitignore, and a main.cc that is exactly 53 lines long. The core idea is already present — cast a ray for each pixel, check whether it hits a sphere, and write a colour. The shading at this point is purely a linear remap of the ray-to-sphere distance: no lighting, no materials, just depth turned into a grey gradient.

What makes this milestone interesting is what is not there yet: there is no Vec3 class (3D vectors are three naked floats), no camera abstraction, no material system, the sky gradient is hardcoded. The image is written using stb_image_write.h, still the output library in use today. The first render shows a single large sphere, obviously not perspective-correct, with depth shading that makes it look like a shaded disc.

First commit message

"first commit" — September 7, 2025

What changed: project scaffolding, CMake, stb_image, first ray–sphere intersection, first rendered pixel.

docs.title: Milestone 2 — Normals, Perspective & Reflections (Sept 8–11, 2025)
docs.text:
Commits: a8f08e7 · 4740f42

Within the first four days, the renderer gains the key ingredients of a recognisable path tracer.

  • Normal-to-colour shading — mapping the surface normal vector to RGB gives the characteristic blue-tinted sphere that features in nearly every "Ray Tracing in One Weekend" tutorial.
  • Camera refactoring — look_from, look_at, and vfov are extracted into a proper class. Perspective is now correct.
  • Reflections — a basic mirror material is added. The timing infrastructure also appears here: each render prints elapsed milliseconds.

By September 11, the scene already has multiple spheres with different materials, and the output image is recognisably a physically-based render rather than a depth map.

What changed: Vec3 class, ray abstraction, camera class, normal-to-RGB shading, mirror reflection, multi-sphere scene, wall-clock timing.

docs.title: Milestone 3 — First CUDA Kernel (Sept 15–16, 2025)
docs.text:
Commit: 671f69d

"Block rendering with CUDA — Final version to be cleaned-up — 38e9 rays in 1 minute"

This is the GPU ignition moment. A first .cu file appears alongside main.cc, and the same sphere scene that was taking seconds on the CPU is handed off to blocks of CUDA threads. The commit message records a key benchmark: 38 thousand rays per minute — not fast by later standards, but proof that the GPU path was working.

The CUDA code at this stage is rough. All scene data is encoded as literals inside the kernel. There is no material system on the GPU side yet — just a hardcoded normal-to-colour calculation mirroring the CPU. The architecture of a separate .cu file talking to a .h host file through an extern "C" boundary — a pattern that scales all the way to the OptiX integration months later — is established here.

However, the two renders (CPU and GPU) look reasonably similar :

The documentation in explanations/CUDA_RENDER_EXPLANATION.md is also written at this commit, showing that the explanation-driven development style starts early.

What changed: first .cu CUDA kernel, GPU ray-sphere intersection, extern "C" host/device boundary, CUDA block/grid launch configuration, first GPU timing measurement.

docs.title: Milestone 4 — Golf Ball & Procedural Displacement (Sept 18–19, 2025)
docs.text:
Commits: 44b3421 · 8f76e3a · 2fa8d0f

"Geo displacement" then "With dots !" then "Very satisfying one"

The first genuinely fun visual moment: a sphere whose surface is perturbed by a procedural displacement function, producing the characteristic dimpled pattern of a golf ball. The commit messages read like a lab notebook — brief, excited, chronological.

The tiled CUDA renderer (rendering the image in tiles rather than all pixels at once) is merged with the regular CUDA path at this point, reducing memory pressure for larger resolutions. A big refactoring pass also separates the two renderers properly so neither needs to know how the other works.

What changed: procedural displacement mapping (Fibonacci dot pattern), tiled CUDA rendering, merged CUDA renderer, renderer separation into distinct compilation units.

docs.title: Milestone 5 — Material System Refactoring (Sept 26, 2025)
docs.text:
Commits: fb88041 · 511956 · 9134c1c

A refactoring week brings the CPU material system to the shape it recognisably holds today. Lambertian diffuse, metals, and a first "constant" (flat-colour) material are given proper abstractions. The parallel CPU renderer gets a progress bar. Normals are now visualisable as colours separately from proper shading.

This is also the point where the CPU path becomes clearly a reference implementation for correctness — run slowly, check against it, trust its output.

What changed: proper Material base class, Lambertian/Metal subclasses, constant material, normal-as-colour diagnostic mode, parallel CPU renderer with progress bar.

docs.title: Milestone 6 — Interactive SDL Window (Nov 3–5, 2025)
docs.text:
Commits: cd710bb · 47da519 · c9bf459

"Add progressive SDL2 rendering with real-time quality improvements" "Add interactive camera controls to SDL progressive rendering" "Even better accumulative samples"

This is one of the most significant feature additions in the project's history: a live SDL2 window that shows the render improving over time. The first version displays the image after each of the sample stages 1 → 4 → 16 → 64 → 256 → 1024, with the user able to press ESC and keep the current quality image. Two days later, interactive camera controls (mouse orbit, pan, scroll-to-zoom) are added.

The renderPixelsSDLProgressive() method — originally just 141 lines in camera.h — becomes the foundation for everything interactive that follows. The key architectural decision made here is that the GPU accumulation buffer lives on the device and is never unnecessarily copied to host until display time; a pattern that contributes directly to the 2× speedup achieved four months later.

What changed: SDL2 window integration, progressive sample-over-time display, interactive camera orbit/pan/zoom, accumulation buffer on device, real-time quality/speed tradeoff.

docs.title: Milestone 7 — The Big November Sprint: BVH, SDF, DOF, Cornell Box (Nov 7, 2025)
docs.text:
Commits (all on the same day): 2dfd645 BVH · 254adfa SDF shapes · 042fc38 SDF rotations · 58b0e34 Depth-of-field · 91f0872 YAML scene loader + Cornell box

AI-assisted development

Three of the five features in this milestone — the SDF procedural shapes, the YAML scene loader, and the Cornell box reference scene — were fully developed with the help of an LLM coding assistant. The BVH and depth-of-field implementations were written hand-in-hand with an LLM.

November 7 is the project's single densest development day. The BVH acceleration structure (Bounding Volume Hierarchy with Surface Area Heuristic), SDF ray-marched procedural shapes, depth-of-field with a thin-lens model, and the YAML scene file loader all land within hours of each other. The classic Cornell box scene also appears as a validation target.

The BVH commit alone adds 833 lines across 7 files, including a full SAH implementation and iterative stack-based GPU traversal. The technical documentation in explanations/BVH_ACCELERATION.md (189 lines) is written in the same commit.

The SDF shapes (torus, octahedron, death-star) use sphere-tracing ray marching on the CPU path. Note that SDF shapes are not currently functional on the GPU — the sphere-tracing loop is not yet ported to the CUDA kernels, so SDF objects are silently skipped during GPU rendering. The rotation support arrives two commits later the same day.

The YAML loader gives scenes a stable, human-readable format that can be shared and versioned alongside the renderer.

What changed: BVH with SAH (CPU build, GPU traversal), SDF procedural shapes with rotations (CPU only), depth of field, YAML scene format, Cornell box reference scene, bvh_test_scene.yaml with 178 objects for performance testing.

docs.title: Milestone 8 — Lambertian Sampling Deep Dive (Nov 13–15, 2025)
docs.text:
Commits: c37a0a1 · ce5c2d1 · dd39b2f

"Lambertian new implementation, using cosine weighted sampling — Included functions for building orthonormal bases" "Refactor Lambertian material to include Owen scrambling for improved randomness and stratification in sampling"

A careful revisit of the Lambertian diffuse model, motivated by discrepancies in the rendered images. Two implementations are compared side by side: the naïve hemisphere sampling and a cosine-weighted version using an orthonormal basis constructed from the surface normal. Owen scrambling — a quasi-random sequence technique — is added to reduce low-frequency noise patterns at low sample counts.

The mathematical foundations for the orthonormal basis construction — in particular the derivation of a consistent local coordinate frame from a single surface normal — were explained by Xavier Richard, whose notes clarified the geometric reasoning behind the Gram–Schmidt approach used here.

This milestone is typical of the educational philosophy behind RayON: not just making it work, but understanding why it works, and documenting the difference an algorithmic choice makes on the output.

What changed: cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling, orthonormal basis construction, Owen scrambling for stratified quasi-random sampling, two-implementation comparison.

docs.title: Milestone 9 — A Name is Born: RayON (Nov 17, 2025)
docs.text:
Commits: a52ee87 · ce66234 · 1b8ff65

"A project name!"

After ten weeks of development under the working title "302_raytracer", the project becomes RayON — a nod to the ray tracing core and the HES-SO Valais backdrop, where the project serves as a teaching vehicle for the CS302 HPC course. The name change is accompanied by the addition of the GNU GPL v3 licence and a major README overhaul.

The clang-tidy static analyser is integrated into the build at this milestone, adding automated code quality checks that run at compile time.

What changed: project renamed to RayON, GPL v3 licence, README rewrite, clang-tidy integration, build system quality-of-life improvements.

docs.title: Milestone 10 — Multi-Platform CUDA (Nov 27, 2025)
docs.text:
Commit: ada3e77

"Tested on AMD64 Linux and fixed for older GPU issue with memory location (no longer shared for RTX2080) — Fixed clangd for Linux ARM64 (ignore CUDA_ARCHITECTURE)"

The renderer is tested on two hardware platforms back to back: an AMD x86-64 Linux machine with an older RTX 2080 GPU, and an ARM64 Linux machine. Both surface different bugs. The RTX 2080 cannot use unified memory for some allocations that worked transparently on newer hardware; those allocations are rerouted. The ARM64 clangd integration requires a guard to skip the CUDA_ARCHITECTURE flag (which is x86-only).

This is the last commit of 2025, representing a natural plateau — the renderer is stable, multi-platform, and has most of its core features.

What changed: RTX 2080 memory allocation fix, ARM64 clangd compatibility, better diagnostics for cross-platform debugging, JSON render statistics with timestamps.

docs.title: Milestone 11 — CUDA 2.24× Speedup & Dear ImGui (March 9–10, 2026)
docs.text:
Commits: 1f5929a · dafa369 · 264e525 · 433000f

"CUDA renderer optimizations: 2.24x speedup (6.08s → 2.71s)" "Replace hand-made SDL GUI with Dear ImGui for interactive renderer"

AI-assisted development

The Dear ImGui integration was implemented entirely by Claude. The CUDA optimisation strategy was worked out collaboratively with Claude — the bottlenecks were identified and the possible improvements discussed together, then some optimisations were implemented by Claude and others by hand.

After a three-month pause, development resumes with an intense performance sprint.

CUDA optimisations (two commits): the D2H (device-to-host) round-trip that was being performed every frame is eliminated. The material array is flattened into a plain struct-of-arrays layout that maps directly to GPU cache lines. BVH traversal is restructured to reduce warp divergence. The result: the benchmark scene drops from 6.08 s to 2.71 s — a 2.24× improvement with no change to output quality.

Dear ImGui replaces the hand-written SDL2 button/slider panel that had been accumulating technical debt since November. The new GUI has collapsible sections, live performance graphs, and proper input capture. SDL2_TTF (font rendering) is dropped as a dependency. The version number jumps to 1.5.0.

What changed: eliminated D2H round-trip, flattened material arrays, reduced BVH warp divergence, Dear ImGui integration with collapsible panels and live SPP/ms graphs, version 1.5.0.

docs.title: Milestone 12 — Adaptive Sampling & Normal Visualisation (March 12, 2026)
docs.text:
Commits: 1bc7183 · 78bd8de · 18c8498

Per-pixel convergence tracking is implemented: each pixel records a running variance estimate and stops accumulating samples early once it has converged. Noisy pixels (typically those with difficult light paths) continue accumulating while already-converged areas freeze. The result is an effective speedup for scenes where some regions converge quickly (flat walls, large lights) while others are slow (specular caustics, glass edges).

The normal arrows overlay arrives in the same few days: a debug visualisation that draws a small 3D arrow from each surface intersection point in the direction of the shading normal. This makes it immediately obvious when a mesh has flipped or missing normals — an invaluable diagnostic for the triangle pipeline work about to begin.

Scene switching from within the interactive GUI is added, allowing different YAML scenes to be loaded and rendered without restarting the program.

What changed: per-pixel adaptive convergence sampling, normal arrows 3D overlay, in-GUI scene switching, scene selection controls in interactive mode.

docs.title: Milestone 13 — Triangle Pipeline & OBJ Loading (March 13, 2026)
docs.text:
Commit: e383e83

"Triangle-based pipeline integration — Added OBJ models rendering and import."

The renderer can now load .obj files and render proper triangle meshes. A Möller–Trumbore intersection test is implemented for triangles on both CPU and GPU. Smooth normals (interpolated from vertex normals in the .obj file) are supported. The Platonic solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron) appear as a showcase scene, each rendered with a different material.

A Python script (generate_platonic_solids.py) generates the .obj files procedurally, and the accompanying YAML scene file wires them together with the new OBJ loader. The project's resources/models/ directory starts filling up.

What changed: triangle.hpp intersection, obj_loader.hpp mesh parser, smooth normal interpolation, five Platonic solid scene files, generate_platonic_solids.py generator.

docs.title: Milestone 14 — Anisotropic Metals, Thin-Film & Clear-Coat (March 13–14, 2026)
docs.text:
Commits: 8623b79 · cca43c1 · 1f7a83d

"Anisotropic metals, stage 1" "Add thin-film interference material and CUDA streams" "Clear-coat and thin-film shading — Car paint, soap bubbles, and demo scenes!"

The most physically rich material work in the project lands in a two-day burst.

Anisotropic metals use a full GGX microfacet BRDF with separate tangential and bitangential roughness parameters. The specular highlight stretches into a horizontal or vertical streak depending on the anisotropy ratio — the effect that makes brushed aluminium look brushed. A dedicated microfacet_ggx.cuh (213 lines) implements the distribution, geometry, and Fresnel terms.

Thin-film interference models the iridescent colour shift seen on soap bubbles, oil films, and camera lenses. The colour of the highlight shifts with viewing angle via an optical path difference calculation over a thin dielectric layer. CUDA streams are added alongside this to overlap kernel execution and memory transfers.

Clear-coat adds a specular dielectric layer on top of a base material — the standard automotive paint model. A Shelby Cobra .obj model and a PokéBall are added to the resources for demonstration.

What changed: GGX anisotropic BRDF, thin-film interference shader, clear-coat multi-layer material, CUDA streams, Shelby Cobra and PokéBall OBJ models, dedicated demo scenes for each material.

docs.title: Milestone 15 — NVIDIA OptiX: Hardware Ray Tracing (March 15, 2026)
docs.text:
Commits: 8ec565e · d831935

"First rendering in OptiX" "First metrics for OptiX: 4x faster for non-interactive rendering on dragon scene! Impressive!"

The final milestone integrates NVIDIA OptiX — the hardware-accelerated ray tracing API that exposes the dedicated RT cores on Turing/Ampere/Ada GPUs. Instead of a custom BVH traversed by CUDA threads, OptiX hands the acceleration structure and traversal off to fixed-function hardware.

The result on the dragon scene (a high-polygon mesh that taxes the BVH heavily): 4× faster than CUDA for offline rendering. The integration is non-trivial: OptiX programs are compiled separately as PTX and loaded at runtime; a new renderer_optix_progressive_host.hpp wraps the OptiX pipeline; all the same material evaluation code is shared with the CUDA path through common .cuh headers.

The OptiX renderer is an optional build target — the renderer detects whether the OptiX SDK is present at CMake time and falls back to CUDA gracefully if it is not.

What changed: full NVIDIA OptiX integration (.ptx programs, OptixPipeline, OptixShaderBindingTable), hardware BVH traversal via RT cores, optional CMake build path, 4× speedup on complex mesh scenes.

docs.title: Milestone 16 — MTL Materials & Image Texture Mapping (March 15–17, 2026)
docs.text:
Commits: ff0a128 · 79793cc · 76be1cf

"Add MTL material loading and diffuse texture support for OBJ meshes" "fix BVH not activating in texture_test scene (20x CUDA speedup)"

AI-assisted development

This milestone was developed with the extensive assistance of an LLM coding agent. The MTL parser, UV propagation pipeline, CUDA/OptiX texture object management were written collaboratively with an AI pair programmer.

The renderer gains the ability to load real image textures and apply them to triangle meshes using UV coordinates from .obj files. Two complementary features land together:

Wavefront MTL support — .obj files can now reference a companion .mtl file that assigns named materials to face groups. The MTL parser (mtl_loader.hpp) reads Kd (diffuse colour), Ke (emission), Ns/Ni (shininess/IOR), and map_Kd (diffuse texture map). A heuristic maps these parameters to the renderer's own material types: dark emitters become LIGHT, high-shininess surfaces become ROUGH_MIRROR or MIRROR, IOR > 1 becomes GLASS, and everything else is LAMBERTIAN.

Image texture mapping — A new texture_loader.cc loads PNG/JPG images via stb_image. The OBJ parser is rewritten to parse vt UV coordinates and propagate them through usemtl groups to individual triangles. On the GPU side, UV values are interpolated across the triangle in hit_triangle() and the resulting (u, v) pair is used to sample a cudaTextureObject_t (CUDA path) or a CUtexObject via OptiX intersection attributes (OptiX path). Texture handles are uploaded to the device once at scene build time and freed on cleanup.

GPU only

Texture mapping is currently implemented for the CUDA and OptiX renderers only. The CPU path renders textured surfaces as flat Lambertian with the material's base colour.

A BVH activation bug in the texture test scene was found and fixed; enabling it produced a 20× CUDA speedup on that scene and is a good reminder that BVH must be explicitly enabled in YAML with use_bvh: true.

New UV-mapped assets shipped with the release: plane_uv.obj, cube_uv.obj, sphere_uv.obj, a checker-grid texture (grid_512.png), and a ready-to-run texture_test.yaml scene.

What changed: mtl_loader.hpp MTL parser, texture_loader.cc stb_image loader, obj_loader.hpp UV + usemtl rewrite, TextureDesc in scene_description.hpp, UV interpolation in CUDA and OptiX backends, cudaTextureObject_t upload/cleanup, UV-mapped OBJ assets, texture_test.yaml scene, generate_uv_models.py script.

docs.title: Milestone 17 — HDR Environment Sky & float16 Optimisation (March 18, 2026)
docs.text:
AI-assisted development

This milestone was developed with the extensive assistance of an LLM coding agent. The equirectangular mapping was made by hand. However, float16 GPU texture upload, binary .hdrcache sidecar, f32_to_f16 clamping fix, and --no-hdr-cache CLI flag were all implemented collaboratively with Claude.

The renderer gains a full HDR environment sky dome: any equirectangular .hdr file from Poly Haven (CC0 licence) can now be loaded as the background sky and sampled during path tracing.

Equirectangular mapping — a ray that misses all scene geometry is mapped to a \((u, v)\) pair using:

\[\theta = \arccos(d_y), \quad \phi = \text{atan2}(-d_z,\; d_x), \quad u = \tfrac{\phi+\pi}{2\pi}, \quad v = \tfrac{\theta}{\pi}\]

Both the CUDA and OptiX backends share a common GPU texture object (cudaTextureObject_t) sampled with bilinear filtering.

float16 GPU textures — the Radiance RGBE source is decoded to 32-bit float then immediately quantised to IEEE 754 half-precision before GPU upload. This halves the VRAM footprint and the PCIe transfer cost compared to a full fp32 texture (e.g. an 8K sky: 512 MB → 256 MB).

Binary .hdrcache sidecar — decoding an 8K .hdr file takes several seconds. On first load the renderer writes a binary sidecar (.hdr.hdrcache) with a 24-byte header and raw fp16 pixels; subsequent launches skip the decode entirely and read the cache directly. Typical improvement: 5–10× faster load times.

fp16 clamping fix — HDR values above 65 504 (the fp16 finite ceiling) are clamped before storage. Without clamping, overflow produces fp16 ±∞ which propagates as NaN through GPU arithmetic and causes occasional pure-black "firefly" pixels. Cache files are versioned; stale v1 caches (created before the fix) are automatically invalidated and regenerated.

Interactive sky switching — in interactive mode, Numpad + / Numpad − cycles through all .hdr files in the directory without restarting the program. A Sky combo-box in the ImGui Environment panel does the same with mouse clicks.

--no-hdr-cache CLI flag bypasses the cache and always re-decodes from the source file (useful when replacing an .hdr file in place during development).

Six HDRIs are bundled (not in git — download via cd resources/hdri && bash download_hdri.sh 8k): venice_sunset, kloppenheim_06, autumn_crossing, studio_small_03, sunflowers_puresky, rosendal_plains_2.

What changed: equirectangular sky dome (CUDA + OptiX), float16 GPU texture format (hdr_env_cache.hpp / hdr_env_cache.cc), binary .hdrcache sidecar with staleness check, fp16 clamping and cache versioning, interactive Numpad sky cycling, ImGui Sky combo-box, --no-hdr-cache CLI flag.

docs.title: Mar 20 — Farewell, CPU renderer
docs.text:
2026-03-20 · e093324

The original CPU rendering backends — single-threaded and multi-threaded — are retired from the main branch. They served as the project's foundation: the very first pixels were rendered one at a time on the CPU, and std::async tiles gave the first taste of parallelism. But with CUDA delivering ~1 000× the throughput and OptiX adding hardware ray tracing on top, the CPU paths had become dead weight — untested, unmaintained, and unused.

The code is preserved on the legacy/cpu-renderer branch for anyone who wants to study the CPU-to-GPU evolution. On main, the cpu_renderers/ directory is gone, rnd_gen.hpp has been relocated to data_structures/, and the normal-arrows overlay (which depended on CPUSceneBuilder) has been removed.

Bye bye!

What changed: deleted src/rayon/cpu_renderers/ (10 files, ~1 800 lines), removed CPU cases from main.cc, stripped CPUSceneBuilder from scene_builder.hpp, removed normal-arrows overlay from both GPU progressive renderers, updated all documentation with archival banners.

docs.title: Milestone 18 — Next Event Estimation & MIS (March 20–21, 2026)
docs.text:
Commits: 104892f (PR #32) · 44b59e9 · 553b912

Until this point the path tracer only found lights by chance: a path bounced off a diffuse surface in a cosine-weighted direction and hoped to land on an emitter. Fine for a sky, hopeless for a small bulb. Milestone 18 adds next event estimation, a shadow ray towards a sampled point on a light at every diffuse hit, and weights it against the BSDF-sampled emitter hits with the power heuristic, so nothing is counted twice. Lights are picked by an area CDF; rectangles are sampled uniformly and spheres by the cone they subtend.

A furnace test scene (15_mis_furnace_test.yaml) checks that the estimator conserves energy, and scripts/render_comparisons.sh produces the sixteen images of the Visual Comparisons page: four scenes, Sobol' against PCG, MIS off against on.

Two clean-up passes follow, the unit tests of the vector math and a dangling ambient-light parameter are removed, and the project goes quiet for seven months.

What changed: NEE and MIS on both GPU back-ends, light tables with area CDFs, shadow-ray traversal, furnace test, comparison renders, --no-mis and --nee-stride.

docs.title: Milestone 19 — OptiX on the RT Cores, Adaptive Sampling Rebuilt (October 27–28, 2026)
docs.text:
Commits: cfac65b · 718afe2 · 36cc0db · 7f4826c

The return starts with correctness: two Sobol' dimensions were correlated in the OptiX sampler, the scramble was not refreshed on restart, polygonal meshes with anisotropic materials showed split faces, and the clear coat was biased under MIS. With those fixed, the OptiX back-end finally uses what it was adopted for: every triangle goes to the RT cores in one hardware geometry acceleration structure, shadow rays terminate on the first hit with a slim payload, and the mesh scenes run at hardware speed.

Adaptive sampling is rebuilt around a standard-error test with smooth re-checks and a consistent firefly clamp, and stops freezing pixels that are lit only by rare bright paths. The interactive window becomes resizable, and a first "motion-time quality scaling" appears. The NEE scene with the tiny bulb (16_nee_small_light.yaml) is added to show what the shadow rays buy, and scripts/rayon_vnc.sh makes the interactive mode usable on a remote GPU server.

What changed: hardware triangles and cheap shadow rays on OptiX, Sobol' fixes, clear-coat MIS fix, adaptive sampling v2, resizable window, NEE demo scene, VNC launcher.

docs.title: Milestone 20 — Camera Motion Regulator & AI Denoiser (October 29, 2026)
docs.text:
Commits: a72647e · db4ade3 · d2c0c87 · 1e96007 · 80c8813

A camera move throws the accumulation away, so an orbit on a heavy scene is a slideshow of one-batch frames. A day of commits turns this into a regulator: while the camera moves the OptiX renderer renders at a fraction of the resolution (quarter, half, three quarters, upscaled for display) with few samples, and a cost model of the previous frames lowers the fraction first and the samples second until the target frame rate holds, then raises them back. The options get their own Camera Motion section in the panel, a display-time despeckle removes the isolated bright dots of the preview, and the OptiX AI denoiser can smooth the motion frames and fade out over the first still ones. None of it touches the converged image.

Adaptive depth, the old trick of starting at four bounces, is retired: the full depth is kept at all times so the lighting does not change character when the camera stops.

What changed: fractional-resolution motion frames, cost-model regulator with target FPS, Camera Motion GUI section, motion despeckle, OptiX denoiser, golf-ball dimple defaults.

docs.title: Milestone 21 — Clouds, SDF Shapes & VDB Data, v1.8.0 (October 30, 2026)
docs.text:
Commits: d3c5795 · 6af216f · bf38756 · b2e07a0 · 2018380

The target image was the cloud bunny of the Physically Based Rendering book. The new volume material turns a closed mesh into a participating medium: a signed distance grid of the mesh built on the GPU, a surface displaced by Worley and fractal noise, a density field baked into a 3D texture, delta tracking with a Henyey–Greenstein phase function, volumetric shadow rays by ratio tracking, all weighted by MIS, with empty-space skipping outside the cloud. The cloud sliders are live in the GUI, and a new button saves the camera and the light settings back into the scene file.

The same day the SDF primitives, which until then were only drawn by the archived CPU renderer, are implemented for both GPU back-ends from one shared marcher (ten shapes, Euler rotations, named parameters, a custom primitive on OptiX), with a studio-room gallery scene. Chasing grain in that scene revealed that next event estimation ran on one sample in three by default; it now runs on every sample. Then the "raw grid" route to OpenVDB data: a Python tool converts a .vdb into a dense grid that the material binds straight into its 3D texture, and the OpenVDB bunny_cloud renders in RayON without any OpenVDB dependency in the C++ code. A per-scene light falloff exponent, time-sized batches for the offline progress bar and a clean-up of the command-line help close the day, and the write-up explanations/VOLUMETRIC_CLOUDS.md turns the remaining work (NanoVDB on the GPU, a grid of local majorants) into a student project.

What changed: volume material and GUI section, cloud bunny scene, save-camera button, SDF primitives on CUDA and OptiX with a gallery scene, visible flag on OptiX, per-scene batch size, NEE stride 1 by default, .vol density grids from OpenVDB, light falloff, offline progress bar, version 1.8.0.

docs.title: Milestone Explorer
docs.text:
Each milestone above has a corresponding commit hash that can be checked out, compiled, and run to experience the renderer at that exact point in its evolution. The script scripts/milestones/goto_milestone.sh handles the full lifecycle automatically:

  1. Stashes any uncommitted work (git stash)
  2. Checks out the milestone commit (detached HEAD)
  3. Configures and builds into a dedicated build_milestone/ directory (never touches your main build/)
  4. Launches the renderer in the appropriate mode for that milestone
  5. Restores the original branch and pops the stash on exit (even on Ctrl+C)
# List all milestones
./scripts/milestones/goto_milestone.sh --list

# Run a milestone in its default mode (offline or interactive SDL)
./scripts/milestones/goto_milestone.sh 7

# Force an offline render even for interactive milestones
./scripts/milestones/goto_milestone.sh 10 --offline

# Leave the repo at the milestone commit after running (for exploration)
./scripts/milestones/goto_milestone.sh 3 --no-restore

docs.text:
The graph below shows how image quality (measured as RMS noise relative to the 4096 SPP reference) improves with sample count. The \(1/\sqrt{N}\) curve is the theoretical Monte Carlo convergence rate.

The \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N})\) convergence is a fundamental property of Monte Carlo integration. Doubling sample count reduces noise by a factor of \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\), meaning halving visible noise requires quadrupling the samples.

docs.title: Tuning tips
docs.text:
• Enable BVH for any scene with more than ~15 objects: use_bvh: true in YAML.
  • Raise the Target FPS in the GUI's "Camera Motion" section for a very responsive orbit/pan experience — the batch size and the render resolution auto-scale down to keep up.
  • Block size — the default 32×8 is tuned for warp alignment; register-cap and block-shape experiments (see ROADMAP.md) gave no consistent gain.
  • Fast math — --use_fast_math is on in Release builds and off in Debug builds.
  • Prefer OptiX (-m 4, -m 5) on RTX-class hardware: triangles and shadow rays run on the RT cores, and the interactive mode has the motion regulator.
  • Keep an eye on the first run after a build: OptiX compiles its module on the first launch (a few seconds, then cached on disk), so time the second run.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
This section explains how RayON is structured internally: how a scene is built and handed to the two GPU back-ends, how the CUDA kernel is launched, and how the interactive renderer accumulates samples and keeps its frame rate.

Scene System

The "build once, render anywhere" design: one neutral SceneDescription converted into flat GPU structs for CUDA and into acceleration structures and a shader binding table for OptiX.

CUDA Renderer

32×8 thread blocks, thread→pixel mapping, random states, the float accumulation buffer, and the C++/CUDA boundary.

Progressive Rendering

The accumulation loop, adaptive sampling, the motion regulator and denoiser, the display pipeline and live parameter updates.

docs.title: CUDA Renderer
docs.text: The CUDA renderer is the primary high-performance back-end. This page explains how a single CUDA kernel maps to image pixels, how memory is managed, and the design choices that make it fast.

docs.title: Thread block shape: 32 × 8
docs.text:
RayON uses a rectangular 2D thread block of 32 columns × 8 rows = 256 threads (16 × 16 on devices that allow fewer than 256 threads per block), and the path-tracing kernel is annotated with __launch_bounds__(256):

dim3 block_size(32, 8);   // 256 threads per block
dim3 grid_size(
    (image_width  + block_size.x - 1) / block_size.x,
    (image_height + block_size.y - 1) / block_size.y
);
renderPixelsKernel<<<grid_size, block_size>>>(...);

Why 32 × 8 instead of, say, 16 × 16?

  • 32 threads per row aligns with one CUDA warp (32 threads that execute in lock-step). Adjacent pixels in the same row touch adjacent memory addresses — the memory access is coalesced and served in one transaction rather than 32 separate ones.
  • 8 rows make 256 threads, which lets the compiler budget registers for a kernel that carries a lot of state (ray, hit record, material, sampler) without spilling.
graph TD
    subgraph "Block (32×8 = 256 threads)"
        direction LR
        row0["Row 0:  pixel [col,   row  ] … pixel [col+31, row  ]  ← 1 warp"]
        row1["Row 1:  pixel [col,   row+1] … pixel [col+31, row+1]  ← 1 warp"]
        rows["…"]
        row7["Row 7:  pixel [col,   row+7] … pixel [col+31, row+7]  ← 1 warp"]
    end
    row0 ~~~ row1 ~~~ rows ~~~ row7

docs.title: Thread → pixel mapping
docs.text:
Each thread computes its pixel coordinates from its block and thread indices:

__global__ void renderPixelsKernel(uint8_t* output, int width, int height, ...) {
    int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;

    if (col >= width || row >= height) return; // guard for non-multiple resolutions

    int pixel_index = row * width + col;
    // ... trace ray for (col, row)
}

docs.title: Random number generation
docs.text:
Every pixel needs independent random numbers. By default they come from a Sobol' sequence with per-pixel Owen scrambling (see Sobol' sampling); the sampler state is stored in the per-pixel curandState slot that the PCG fallback also uses:

// Initialisation — called once per pixel on first launch
curand_init(
    (unsigned long long)(row * width + col),  // unique seed per pixel
    0,                                          // sequence offset
    0,                                          // subsequence
    &rng_states[pixel_index]
);

The rng_state array lives in device memory and is reused across accumulative frames — re-initialising it every frame would reset the random sequence and cause visible patterns. For the one-shot renderer, states are allocated, used, then freed.

docs.title: Accumulation buffer
docs.text:
For progressive (multi-sample) rendering, simply averaging uint8 RGB values loses precision. RayON keeps a float accumulation buffer on the GPU:

// Device memory — 3 floats per pixel (per channel running sum)
float* d_accumulation_buffer; // RGB, float per channel
cudaMalloc(&d_accumulation_buffer, width * height * 3 * sizeof(float));

After each kernel pass, the float sums are normalised and gamma-corrected on the GPU:

__global__ void gammaCorrectKernel(const float* accum, uint8_t* display, int num_pixels, int spp) {
    int idx = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (idx >= num_pixels) return;

    float r = sqrtf(accum[idx*3 + 0] / spp); // sqrt = gamma 2.0 correction
    float g = sqrtf(accum[idx*3 + 1] / spp);
    float b = sqrtf(accum[idx*3 + 2] / spp);

    display[idx*3 + 0] = (uint8_t)(clamp(r, 0.f, 1.f) * 255.f);
    display[idx*3 + 1] = (uint8_t)(clamp(g, 0.f, 1.f) * 255.f);
    display[idx*3 + 2] = (uint8_t)(clamp(b, 0.f, 1.f) * 255.f);
}

Only the compact uint8 display buffer (3 bytes/pixel) is copied device → host. The accumulation buffer stays on the GPU until the session ends.

This eliminates the round-trip that previously transferred the full float buffer each frame — a 4× reduction in D2H bandwidth.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Every CUDA API call is wrapped with CUDA_CHECK():

// From cuda_utils.cuh
#define CUDA_CHECK(call)                                                   \
    do {                                                                   \
        cudaError_t err = (call);                                          \
        if (err != cudaSuccess) {                                          \
            fprintf(stderr, "CUDA error %s:%d — %s\n",                   \
                    __FILE__, __LINE__, cudaGetErrorString(err));          \
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);                                            \
        }                                                                  \
    } while (0)

// Usage
CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&d_scene, sizeof(CudaScene::Scene)));
CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(d_scene, &h_scene, sizeof(CudaScene::Scene), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));

For kernel launches, the error check happens after synchronisation:

myKernel<<<grid, block>>>(...);
CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetLastError());      // catches launch errors
CUDA_CHECK(cudaDeviceSynchronize()); // waits for completion, surfaces kernel errors

docs.title: C++ ↔ CUDA boundary
docs.text:
RayON keeps CUDA in .cu files and exposes a plain C++ interface via extern "C" or thin wrapper headers. The Camera class calls GPU code via:

// renderer_cuda_host.hpp (C++)
extern void renderPixelsCUDAAccumulative(
    const CudaScene::Scene* d_scene,
    float*                  d_accum,
    curandState*            d_rng,
    int width, int height,
    int sample_count
);

The implementation lives in renderer_cuda_device.cu and is compiled by nvcc. The CMake target links the .cu object with CUDA_SEPARABLE_COMPILATION ON so that device functions defined in separate .cu files can call each other.

docs.title: Device properties caching
docs.text:
Querying device properties (SM count, clock rate, etc.) is expensive. RayON caches the cudaDeviceProp struct once at startup:

// Called once at init
cudaGetDeviceProperties(&g_device_props, 0);

// Later, fast read
int sm_count = g_device_props.multiProcessorCount; // no API call
