docs.text: Flag Effect -O3 Host-side optimisation --expt-relaxed-constexpr Allow constexpr host functions in device code -lineinfo (Debug) Source-level line info for cuda-gdb and Nsight --use_fast_math (Release) Fast rsqrtf, fused multiply-add, relaxed denormals CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native Compiled for the GPU of the build machine OptiX PTX optix_programs.cu is compiled to PTX at -O3 (with -lineinfo in Debug) and loaded at run time

docs.title: Progressive Rendering
docs.text: The interactive modes (3 for CUDA, 5 for OptiX) are where RayON feels most alive. This page explains how the accumulation loop keeps the window responsive while the image converges, and how the OptiX renderer holds its frame rate while the camera moves.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The interactive host (renderer_optix_progressive_host.hpp, renderer_cuda_progressive_host.hpp) runs one loop:

  1. Poll SDL events: mouse, keyboard, window resize, the Dear ImGui panel.
  2. If the camera or a scene parameter changed, reset the accumulation (zero the float buffer on the device, restart the sample counter).
  3. Launch one batch of samples per pixel on the GPU and add it to the accumulation buffer.
  4. Convert the buffer to the 8-bit display image on the GPU, copy it to pinned host memory, upload it to the SDL texture, draw the panel, present.
sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant SDL
    participant Host as Host (C++)
    participant GPU
    User->>SDL: drag the mouse
    SDL-->>Host: SDL_MOUSEMOTION
    Host->>GPU: reset accumulation (memset on the render stream)
    loop every frame
        Host->>GPU: launch(samples_per_batch, samples_so_far)
        GPU-->>Host: uint8 display buffer (async copy, pinned memory)
        Host->>SDL: SDL_UpdateTexture + SDL_RenderCopy + ImGui
        SDL-->>User: frame
    end

There is no fixed schedule of sample stages and no pause between batches: as long as the camera is still, every frame adds Samples/Batch samples (8 by default, per-scene override with settings.samples_per_batch), until the accumulation is complete.

docs.title: Float accumulation on the GPU
docs.text:
The accumulation buffer is a float4 array of width × height that never leaves the device. Each kernel launch adds its samples to it and keeps the total count; a small gamma kernel then converts the running mean to 8-bit RGB:

float r = sqrtf(accum[i].x / total_samples);   // gamma 2.0 = sqrt

Only the 3-byte-per-pixel display image crosses to the host, through an asynchronous copy into page-locked memory on a dedicated stream, so the next batch can start while the previous frame is being displayed (see Optimisations, items 7, 11 and 17).

The sampler state (Sobol' index, scramble seed) is also persistent per pixel, and the scramble is refreshed on every restart so that consecutive accumulations do not replay the same sequence.

docs.title: When does it stop?
docs.text: Condition Default Adaptive sampling reports 99.9 % of the pixels converged on The per-pixel budget is reached 100 000 samples Accumulation paused with Space or --no-auto-accumulate —

docs.title: Adaptive sampling
docs.text: Each pixel tracks its own sample count and the statistics of its value. After 32 samples, a pixel whose standard error in display space falls below the threshold (0.01 of the 0–1 range, about 2.5 levels of 255, adjustable in the GUI) is flagged as converged and skipped by later batches; the GPU counts the converged pixels with a warp-shuffle reduction so only one integer comes back to the host. Pixels that are lit only by rare bright paths keep sampling. The Show Sample Heatmap option paints the samples spent per pixel.

docs.title: Camera motion (OptiX)
docs.text:
A camera move invalidates the accumulation, so during an orbit every frame is a one-batch image. At full resolution that is a few frames per second on a heavy scene. The OptiX host therefore trades quality for frame rate while the camera moves only:

flowchart LR
    A["camera event"] --> B["moving: render at a fraction of the
resolution with few samples,
upscale for display"]
    B -->|"no event for the cooldown (50 ms)"| C["still: full resolution,
Samples/Batch per frame,
accumulate"]
    C -->|"camera event"| B

The regulator holds a target frame rate (60 fps by default). It models the cost of a motion frame from the previous ones and, when the frame rate drops, lowers the render fraction first (from the ceiling of 3/4 down to a floor of 1/4 of the width and height, that is 1/16 of the pixels), then the samples per frame (down to a floor of 4). When there is headroom it raises them back. Every value is a slider in the Camera Motion section of the panel; the readout shows what the last motion frame used.

On top of the regulator, the motion frames can use one sample per pixel, the cheaper PCG sampler, a capped bounce depth, skip the shadow rays, be despeckled at display time, and be passed through the OptiX AI denoiser (guided by the albedo and normal of the first hit). The denoiser can keep running over the first still frames with a weight that fades to zero at 64 samples, so the image does not snap from smooth to noisy when the camera stops. Optional intermediate stages (1/2 then 3/4 resolution, each fading into the previous image) are available for very heavy scenes.

The CUDA interactive renderer has none of this: it keeps rendering full batches while the camera moves, with the display-time despeckle as its only concession.

docs.title: Camera interaction
docs.text:
Input Action Left mouse + drag Orbit around the look-at point Right mouse + drag Pan the camera and the look-at point Scroll wheel Zoom O Auto orbit Left / Right Previous / next scene

The orbit keeps the camera on a sphere around the look-at point in spherical coordinates; the pan moves both points along the camera's right and up vectors. Any change restarts the accumulation; the GUI's Save camera & lights button writes the current view into the scene file.

docs.title: Live parameter updates
docs.text:
Most sliders change a value that is passed to the next launch and restart the accumulation. Nothing is rebuilt:

  • OptiX: background intensity, light intensity and falloff, depth of field, the MIS and sampler options are fields of the launch parameters, uploaded (a few hundred bytes) before every launch. The cloud sliders rewrite one material record and re-bake its density field.
  • CUDA: the same values are __constant__ symbols updated with cudaMemcpyToSymbol, and the material record is rewritten in place.

Changing the scene rebuilds everything: the acceleration structures, the material and light tables, the textures and the volume grids.

The interactive window on the DGX Spark. The panel on the right holds every setting of this page.

docs.title: Scene System
docs.text: RayON uses a "build once, render anywhere" architecture. A single host-side scene description is constructed once, from YAML or from C++, and handed to whichever GPU back-end renders it.

docs.title: The core idea
docs.text:
GPU kernels cannot use virtual functions, heap allocation, or polymorphism. RayON uses one neutral representation (Scene::SceneDescription) that is converted into the GPU-specific flat format at build time:

flowchart LR
    yaml["YAML file\nor\nC++ code"]
    desc["SceneDescription\n(host-side, neutral)"]
    gpu_builder["CudaSceneBuilder\n::buildGPUScene()"]
    gpu_scene["CudaScene::Scene\n(flat GPU structs)"]
    optix_builder["optixRendererBuildScene()\nbuildGAS()"]
    optix_scene["OptiX GAS + IAS\nSBT records, light table"]

    yaml -->|parse / construct| desc
    desc --> gpu_builder --> gpu_scene
    desc --> optix_builder --> optix_scene

    style desc fill:#2d3436,stroke:#e17055,color:#ffffff

docs.title: SceneDescription
docs.text:
Defined in src/rayon/scenes/scene_description.hpp, SceneDescription holds:

  • Materials — a std::vector<MaterialDesc>: a type enum and every parameter any type may need (albedo, roughness, complex IOR, film thickness, volume density and noise, grid file…)
  • Geometry — a std::vector<GeometryDesc> with a type enum and a parameters union; an OBJ mesh becomes one TRIANGLE entry per face
  • BVH nodes — built by buildBVH() with the surface area heuristic, a flat std::vector<BVHNode>
  • Camera and settings — position, look-at, field of view, background colour and intensity, light intensity and falloff, batch size, the path of the YAML file the scene came from
  • Textures — image paths, deduplicated, uploaded once per back-end

docs.title: Adding objects programmatically
docs.text:
// Create a scene
Scene::SceneDescription scene_desc;

// Add a material
int gold = scene_desc.addMaterial(
    MaterialDesc::roughMirror(Vec3(1.0, 0.85, 0.57), /*roughness=*/0.03)
);

// Add a sphere using that material
scene_desc.addSphere(Vec3(-2.0, 0.5, 0.0), /*radius=*/0.8, gold);

// Add a rectangle area light
int light = scene_desc.addMaterial(MaterialDesc::light(Vec3(5, 4.5, 3.5)));
scene_desc.addRectangle(Vec3(-1, 3, -2), Vec3(2.5, 0, 0), Vec3(0, 0, 1.5), light);

// Enable BVH
scene_desc.use_bvh = true;

This is how scene_factory.hpp builds the built-in default scene; yaml_scene_loader.cc does the same from a file and can write the camera and light settings back into it.

docs.title: CUDA scene building
docs.text:
CudaSceneBuilder::buildGPUScene(desc) converts the description into Plain Old Data structures the GPU can work with:

// From scene_builder_cuda.cu
void convertGeometry(const GeometryDesc& g, CudaScene::Geometry& out) {
    out.type = static_cast<CudaScene::GeometryType>(g.type);
    if (g.type == GeometryType::SPHERE) {
        out.sphere.center = make_float3(g.sphere.center);
        out.sphere.radius = (float)g.sphere.radius;
    }
    // ... other types
}

The result is a CudaScene::Scene struct containing:

  • Geometry* geometries — flat array of POD geometry structs
  • Material* materials — flat array of POD material structs
  • BVHNode* bvh_nodes — flat array (if BVH is enabled)
  • int num_geometries, int num_materials, int num_bvh_nodes

All of these are allocated with cudaMalloc and freed after rendering. Volume materials get their signed distance grid and baked density field built here (volume_sdf.cu), as 3D textures bound into the material.

docs.title: OptiX scene building
docs.text:
optixRendererBuildScene() walks the same description but splits it by how OptiX intersects things: every TRIANGLE goes into one triangle geometry acceleration structure handled by the RT cores, with a per-triangle side table (material, normals, UVs, visibility); spheres, rectangles, displaced spheres and SDF shapes become custom primitives with their own bounding boxes and a shader binding table record each. A one-level instance acceleration structure references both. Volumes are traced as a box around their mesh. Lights are collected into a device table with an area CDF for next event estimation.

CPU renderers archived

The CPU back-ends and their CPUSceneBuilder live on the legacy/cpu-renderer branch.

docs.title: Type discrimination on the GPU
docs.text:
Without virtual functions, the GPU dispatcher uses switch statements:

// From cuda_raytracer.cuh
__device__ bool intersect_geometry(const Geometry& g, const Ray& r, float t_min, float t_max,
                                   HitRecord& rec) {
    switch (g.type) {
        case GeometryType::SPHERE:
            return intersect_sphere(g.sphere, r, t_min, t_max, rec);
        case GeometryType::RECTANGLE:
            return intersect_rectangle(g.rect, r, t_min, t_max, rec);
        case GeometryType::SDF_PRIMITIVE:
            return intersect_sdf(g.sdf, r, t_min, t_max, rec);
        // ...
    }
    return false;
}

The same pattern is used for material evaluation:

__device__ void scatter_material(const Material& mat, ...) {
    switch (mat.type) {
        case MaterialType::LAMBERTIAN: scatter_lambertian(...); break;
        case MaterialType::ROUGH_MIRROR: scatter_rough_mirror(...); break;
        case MaterialType::GLASS: scatter_glass(...); break;
        // ...
    }
}

docs.title: Memory layout decisions
docs.text:
The BVHNode is padded to exactly 64 bytes — one cache line — so that a single L2 cache line access fetches one complete node. This is critical for GPU BVH traversal performance, where tree lookups are the primary memory bottleneck.

For float vs. double: the host builds everything in double precision (standard C++), and precision is reduced to float at the GPU kernel boundary. This choice avoids precision artefacts in scene geometry construction while keeping GPU compute on float lanes.

docs.title: Adding a new geometry type
docs.text:
1. Add the enum value to GeometryType in scenes/scene_description.hpp.
  2. Add a parameters struct inside the GeometryDesc union and a SceneDescription::addMyShape() factory method that fills the bounds.
  3. Add a CudaScene::Geometry union member in cuda_scene.cuh and the convertGeometry() case in scene_builder_cuda.cu.
  4. Implement the intersection in cuda_raytracer.cuh (intersect_geometry()), ideally in a header shared with OptiX as sdf_primitives.cuh is.
  5. On OptiX, add an __intersection__ program in optix_programs.cu, a program group and the SBT record fill in optix_renderer.cu, and list the type in buildGAS().
  6. Parse it in yaml_scene_loader.cc and document it in SCENE_FORMAT.md.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Practical documentation: how to use each capability, which options exist, and where they live in the YAML format or the GUI.

Interactive Mode

The SDL2 window: mouse orbit, pan and zoom, keyboard shortcuts, every panel of the Dear ImGui control panel, the motion regulator and the AI denoiser.

YAML Scene Format

Camera, settings, materials, geometry, procedural patterns, the visible flag, and the button that writes the camera back into the file.

Lights & Shadows

Rectangle and sphere lights, hidden emitters, next event estimation, the light intensity and falloff controls, and the scene that shows what NEE buys.

Volumes, Clouds & Smoke

The volume material: a scattering medium inside a mesh, shaped by procedural noise or by an OpenVDB density grid, with volumetric shadow rays.

SDF Shapes

Ten ray-marched signed distance primitives, from the torus to the mandelbulb, with rotation and named parameters, on both back-ends.

OBJ Mesh Loading

Wavefront meshes with MTL materials, smooth normals and UV textures; hardware triangles on OptiX, a per-triangle BVH on CUDA.

HDR Sky Dome

Equirectangular HDRI environments as the sky, cycled at runtime, stored as float16 textures with a binary disk cache; the OptiX interactive mode samples the sun directly (sky importance sampling).

docs.title: HDR Sky Dome
docs.text: RayON supports two sky models: a built-in procedural gradient (zero setup required) and a full HDR environment map loaded from an .hdr file and projected as an equirectangular sky dome.

docs.title: Built-in gradient sky
docs.text:
By default the sky is a vertical gradient from white at the horizon to background_color at the zenith, scaled by background_intensity (the GUI's Ambient Light):

settings:
  background_color: [0.45, 0.65, 0.95]   # zenith colour (default: [0.5, 0.7, 1.0])
  background_intensity: 0.25             # 0 = no sky light at all

This sky needs no image file and costs nothing.

docs.title: HDR environment sky dome
docs.text:
An equirectangular .hdr file (Radiance RGBE format) is mapped onto an infinite sphere around the scene. Any ray that misses all geometry samples the sky dome in its direction.

The sky is chosen in the interactive modes, not in the scene file: at start-up the renderer scans resources/hdri/ (looked up as ../resources/hdri from build/) and lists every .hdr it finds in the Sky combo of the Environment & Materials section, after the built-in gradient. Numpad + / − cycle through them. The offline modes render with the gradient sky.

The mapping is derived from the ray's unit direction vector:

\[\theta = \arccos(d_y), \quad \phi = \text{atan2}(-d_z,\; d_x)$$ $$u = \frac{\phi + \pi}{2\pi}, \quad v = \frac{\theta}{\pi}\]

The resulting $ (u, v) \in [0,1]^2 $ coordinates index into the equirectangular texture, with \(v = 0\) at the north pole and \(v = 1\) at the south pole.

docs.title: Switching sky in interactive mode
docs.text:
Input Effect Numpad + or = Next HDRI of the directory Numpad − or − Previous HDRI Sky combo Pick any file by name; the first entry is the built-in gradient --sky <name> Command line: start with the first file whose name contains <name> (--sky sunflowers) settings.hdr_sky Scene file: the sky to show when this scene is loaded (hdr_sky: "venice_sunset"), the gradient without it; --sky wins at start-up

Switching takes the decode time of the file the first time (seconds for an 8K map), then the .hdrcache sidecar makes it near instant.

docs.title: Downloading the HDRI files
docs.text:
The bundled HDRIs are sourced from Poly Haven under the CC0 licence. Because each file is 25–250 MB, they are not included in the repository. A download script is provided:

# Download 8K HDRIs (recommended quality)
cd resources/hdri
bash download_hdri.sh 8k

# Or lower resolutions
bash download_hdri.sh 2k
bash download_hdri.sh 4k

The six bundled environments:

Environment Source venice_sunset polyhaven.com/a/venice_sunset kloppenheim_06 polyhaven.com/a/kloppenheim_06 autumn_crossing polyhaven.com/a/autumn_crossing studio_small_03 polyhaven.com/a/studio_small_03 sunflowers_puresky polyhaven.com/a/sunflowers_puresky rosendal_plains_2 polyhaven.com/a/rosendal_plains_2

Adding your own HDRIs

Any equirectangular .hdr file works: put it in resources/hdri/ and it appears in the Sky combo at the next start.

A very bright sun disk in an HDR map is the classic firefly source: in sunflowers_puresky the sun covers 0.08 millisteradian, about 180 texels of the 8K map, yet carries 45 % of the sky's energy. The OptiX interactive mode samples the sky directly (see Sky importance sampling below), so the sun lights diffuse surfaces through shadow rays and casts proper shadows instead of being found by chance. The CUDA interactive mode has no sky sampling: a diffuse bounce hits the sun once in about 40 000 samples, each hit worth tens of thousands, and only the luminance clamp (a fixed ceiling of 20 while the camera moves, a growing one when still, see Lights & Shadows) keeps the speckle in check. It never converges there: the clamp grows with the square root of the sample count and the hits arrive in proportion to it, so the speckle keeps a constant amplitude.

docs.title: Sky importance sampling
docs.text:
OptiX interactive mode only. When an HDR map is uploaded, buildEnvSamplingTables() (optix_renderer.cu) reduces it to a grid of at most 2048 × 1024 cells (a 4 × 4 texel box on an 8K map) weighted by luminance × sin θ, the solid angle of a lat-long cell, and builds a 2D distribution over it: a marginal CDF over the rows and one conditional CDF per row. The tables are accumulated in double precision and stored as float, so the probability of a cell is exactly the difference of two consecutive CDF entries, on the sampling side as on the pdf side.

The sky then takes part in next-event estimation like a light: sample_env_optix() picks a row from the marginal CDF, a cell from that row, a uniform direction inside the cell and returns its radiance with the solid-angle pdf

\[p_\Omega(u, v) = \frac{p_\text{row} \, p_\text{cell} \, W H}{2\pi^2 \sin\theta}\]

where \(2\pi^2 \sin\theta\) is the Jacobian of the lat-long mapping. When the scene also has emitters, half of the NEE samples go to the sky and half to the light list, and every pdf carries that selection probability. A BSDF-sampled ray that escapes to the sky is weighted by the power heuristic against env_pdf_optix() of its direction, exactly as an emitter hit is weighted against the light pdf, so the sun is never counted twice. Samples drawn below the surface skip the shadow ray. Everything is tied to the Enable MIS toggle: with MIS off the sky is left to BSDF sampling, as before.

Measured on the default scene under sunflowers_puresky after 30 s at 720p: the speckle count drops by a factor of 30 and the image is 20 % brighter, the sun's share that the luminance clamp was holding back. The remaining dots are sun caustics: the sun reaching a diffuse surface through the glass sphere or off the metal sphere, paths that no light sampling can reach (the same scene with those two spheres made diffuse shows none). They are held down by the indirect clamp. The cost is the shadow ray of each diffuse bounce (about a quarter of the frame rate on that scene, which had no emitter and therefore no shadow rays before).

docs.title: float16 GPU texture
docs.text:
The .hdr file is decoded from Radiance RGBE (four bytes per pixel) to 32-bit float triplets by stb_image, then each channel is converted to IEEE 754 float16 (half precision). The resulting four-channel half-float image is uploaded to a cudaTextureObject_t with format:

cudaChannelFormatDesc{16, 16, 16, 16, cudaChannelFormatKindFloat}

CUDA hardware automatically promotes the fp16 values to fp32 on tex2D<float4> fetch — no shader-side conversion is needed.

Memory impact:

Resolution Uncompressed fp32 (VRAM) fp16 VRAM Saving 2K (2048 × 1024) 32 MB 16 MB 50 % 4K (4096 × 2048) 128 MB 64 MB 50 % 8K (8192 × 4096) 512 MB 256 MB 50 %

docs.title: Binary disk cache (.hdrcache)
docs.text:
Loading and decoding an 8K .hdr file (≈ 200 MB on disk) takes several seconds. On subsequent launches, the renderer writes a binary sidecar next to the .hdr file (e.g. venice_sunset_8k.hdr.hdrcache) and reads it on the next run.

A .hdrcache file is a compact binary blob with a 24-byte header followed by the raw fp16 pixel data — no decompression or format conversion needed. Typical time savings: 5–10× faster loads compared to re-decoding the RGBE source.

┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  magic  │  version  │  w  │  h  │  (16 bytes)
│            source_size          │  (8 bytes, staleness check)
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  width × height × 4 × uint16_t │  (raw fp16 pixels, RGBA order)
└─────────────────────────────────┘

The source file's byte-size is stored in the header. If the .hdr file is replaced or modified (size changes), the cache is automatically invalidated and regenerated.

To skip the cache entirely (e.g. for diagnostics):

./rayon --no-hdr-cache --scene ../resources/scenes/default_scene.yaml

docs.title: fp16 clamping
docs.text:
HDR scene radiance values can exceed the fp16 finite range (65 504). Values above this threshold are clamped to ±65504 before storage — ensuring the GPU texture never receives ±∞, which would propagate as NaN during path-tracing arithmetic and produce black "firefly" pixels.

Stale cache files

If you have .hdrcache files created by an older version of RayON (before the clamping fix), delete them and let the renderer regenerate them. Newly generated caches are identified by a version field in the header and will be automatically regenerated when the version does not match.

docs.title: Interactive Mode
docs.text: Modes 3 (CUDA) and 5 (OptiX) open an SDL2 window where any scene can be explored in real time: mouse-driven camera, progressive accumulation, and a Dear ImGui panel holding every rendering parameter. Mode 5 is the default when the OptiX SDK is available; it is also the one with the motion regulator and the AI denoiser.

docs.title: Starting interactive mode
docs.text:
cd build
./rayon --scene ../resources/scenes/17_cloud_bunny.yaml        # mode 5 (or 3 without OptiX)
./rayon -m 3 --scene ../resources/scenes/09_color_bleed_box.yaml

SDL2 required

The interactive modes exist only when SDL2 was found at CMake configure time. On a remote GPU server, run the window through VNC with scripts/rayon_vnc.sh (see Getting Started).

docs.title: Camera controls
docs.text:
Input Effect Left mouse + drag Orbit around the look-at point Right mouse + drag Pan the camera and the look-at point Scroll wheel Zoom (distance to the look-at point) O Auto orbit

Any camera change restarts the accumulation.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text: Key Effect Space Pause or resume the accumulation Left / Right Previous / next scene (every YAML file of resources/scenes/) Numpad + / − (or = / −) Next / previous HDR sky N Toggle the normal visualisation F Toggle the samples-per-second counter L Toggle the logo H Hide / show the panel Enter Collapse / expand the panel window C Collapse / expand every section R Reset the light, material and camera settings to their defaults Esc Quit

docs.title: How accumulation works
docs.text:
Each frame adds a batch of Samples/Batch samples to every pixel (8 by default; a scene can set settings.samples_per_batch, and --samples-per-batch on the command line wins). The samples go into a float accumulation buffer that stays on the GPU; a small kernel converts it to the 8-bit display image.

While the camera is still, the renderer keeps adding batches until one of these happens:

  • Adaptive sampling reports that 99.9 % of the pixels have converged (see below),
  • the budget of 100 000 samples per pixel is reached,
  • you pause it with Space, or started with --no-auto-accumulate.

While the camera moves, the OptiX renderer trades quality for frame rate (see Camera Motion below). The CUDA renderer keeps rendering full batches.

docs.title: The control panel
docs.text: The panel sits at the right of the window. Every section is a collapsible header.

docs.title: Scene
docs.text: The scene combo lists every YAML file found in resources/scenes/; the arrow keys cycle through it. The current camera position and look-at point are displayed, and the button Save camera & lights to scene YAML writes them back into the file the scene was loaded from, together with the light settings. Only the camera: lines (position, look_at, fov) and the settings: keys background_intensity, light_intensity, light_falloff (and indirect_clamp on OptiX) are rewritten; comments and everything else are kept. This is how the bundled scenes got their viewpoints.

docs.title: Adaptive Sampling
docs.text:
Control Default Effect Adaptive Sampling on After 32 samples, a pixel whose standard error falls below the threshold stops taking samples Threshold 0.01 Standard error of the displayed value, in levels of 255 (about 2.5 levels) Show Sample Heatmap off Plasma colour map of the samples spent per pixel (purple = few, yellow = many)

docs.title: MIS / NEE
docs.text: Enable MIS (master toggle for next event estimation and the MIS weights), NEE stride (beyond the first bounce, shadow rays on 1 of every N samples, 1 by default) and the Sobol sampler checkbox (uncheck for PCG). See Multiple Importance Sampling.

docs.title: Camera Motion (OptiX)
docs.text:
Everything in this section applies only while the camera moves. The accumulation restarts on every move, so none of it changes the final image.

Control Default Effect Max while moving 3/4 Highest fraction of the width and height rendered while moving; the frame is upscaled for display Hold a target frame rate on, 60 fps The regulator lowers the render fraction first, then the samples per frame, until the frame rate holds, and raises them back when there is headroom Min while moving 1/4 Floor of the render fraction (1/16 of the pixels) Min samples 4 Floor of the samples per pixel per motion frame; Samples/Batch is the ceiling Intermediate stages off When the camera stops, climb through 1/2 and 3/4 resolution before full, with a stage length, a fade and a motion cooldown One sample per frame off Ignore the batch size while moving Fast sampler (PCG) off PCG instead of Sobol' while moving Limit bounce depth off Cap the bounces at 4 while moving (about 10 % faster, indirect light slightly darker) Disable MIS / NEE while moving off Skip the shadow rays while moving (--motion-gate-mis) Despeckle motion frames on, ratio 2 At display time, a pixel far brighter than its 8 neighbours is scaled down; the accumulation is untouched AI denoiser (OptiX) off Run the OptiX neural denoiser on every motion frame, guided by the albedo and normal of the first hit. Display only. Fade out until (64 spp) keeps denoising the first still frames with a weight that fades to zero, so the image does not snap from smooth to noisy

The readout under the sliders shows the resolution fraction and the samples used by the last motion frame, and the denoiser time when it runs.

docs.title: Display pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Path tracing kernel\n(CUDA or OptiX)"] -->|adds a batch of samples| B["float4 accumulation buffer\n(device memory)"]
    B -->|gamma kernel, upscale of motion frames| C["uint8 display buffer\n(device memory)"]
    C -->|async copy to pinned host memory| D["uint8 host buffer"]
    D -->|SDL_UpdateTexture| E["SDL texture"]
    E -->|SDL_RenderCopy| F["Window"]

Only three bytes per pixel cross from the device to the host each frame, about 6 MB at 1920×1080. The float accumulation buffer never leaves the GPU.

docs.title: Lights & Shadows
docs.text: Lights in RayON are ordinary geometry carrying a light material. Rectangles and spheres are sampled explicitly by next event estimation, which is what turns a tiny bright bulb from a firefly generator into clean, soft shadows at a handful of samples per pixel.

docs.title: Emitters
docs.text:
materials:
  - name: "sun"
    type: "light"
    emission: [300.0, 285.0, 255.0]        # linear radiance, any magnitude

  - name: "warm_light"
    type: "light"
    color: [1.0, 0.875, 0.75]              # or a colour …
    emission_intensity: 12                 # … times a scalar

geometry:
  - type: "rectangle"                      # area light
    material: "warm_light"
    corner: [-1.5, 4, -1.5]
    u: [3, 0, 0]
    v: [0, 0, 3]

  - type: "sphere"                         # bulb
    material: "sun"
    center: [-42, 26, 14]
    radius: 4
    visible: false                         # lights the scene, not seen by camera rays

The emission is radiance: a small light needs a large value to deliver the same power as a large panel. The comment in 16_nee_small_light.yaml shows the arithmetic for swapping a 12 cm square panel for a 6 cm bulb.

docs.title: Hidden emitters
docs.text: visible: false hides an object from camera rays only. It still casts light, shadows and shows in reflections. Both back-ends honour the flag. The cloud scenes use it for the sun, the SDF gallery for a large soft box above the room.

docs.title: Next event estimation
docs.text:
Every non-specular hit traces one shadow ray towards a point sampled on a light: a light is picked with probability proportional to its power (area × luminance of its emission) on OptiX, to its area on CUDA, then a point on it (uniform on rectangles, inside the visible cone for spheres). The emitter's contribution is weighted against the chance that the material's own scattering would have found it, so that nothing is counted twice. This is multiple importance sampling; the math is on the MIS page.

On OptiX, Lambertian, clear-coat and SDF-material surfaces take shadow rays; mirrors, glass, anisotropic metals and thin films are treated as specular and skip them. The CUDA back-end samples lights for Lambertian surfaces. Volumes trace shadow rays from every scattering event, through the medium itself (Volumes).

Option Where Default Enable MIS GUI MIS / NEE, --no-mis on NEE stride GUI, --nee-stride <N> 1 (every sample; the first bounce always traces its shadow ray) Disable while the camera moves GUI Camera Motion, --motion-gate-mis off

docs.title: What it buys
docs.text:
16_nee_small_light.yaml: five matte spheres in a dark room under a 6 cm bulb. Render it at 4 samples per pixel with and without MIS:

./rayon -m 4 -s 4 --scene ../resources/scenes/16_nee_small_light.yaml
./rayon -m 4 -s 4 --scene ../resources/scenes/16_nee_small_light.yaml --no-mis

Without explicit light sampling, almost no random bounce hits a 6 cm sphere, so the image is black with sparse white speckles. With it, the shadows are already readable. Both converge to the same image at high sample counts. The Visual Comparisons page shows the effect on four scenes with a slider.

docs.title: Light intensity and falloff
docs.text:
Two per-scene settings adjust all the lights at once, live from the GUI, saved with the camera.

Setting GUI Default Effect light_intensity Lights inten. 1 Multiplier on every emission light_falloff Lights falloff 2 Distance exponent of the lights' reach indirect_clamp Indirect clamp 50 OptiX: per-sample ceiling on indirect light, 0 = off (see Fireflies)

The falloff is an artistic control layered over the physics. Sphere and rectangle lights already follow the inverse square law through the geometry; the setting multiplies every light contribution at distance \(d\) by

\[ d^{\,2 - \text{falloff}} \]

so nothing changes at one scene unit from the light. At 1 the light carries farther and a dark room opens up; at 3 or 4 it dies out around the source and the scene becomes a bulb in the dark. The factor is applied to the shadow rays and to the emitter hits of scattered paths alike, which keeps MIS consistent; camera rays see the emitters unchanged. It is not energy conserving, and it applies to the volumetric shadow rays too, so a sun 50 units away reacts strongly to it.

settings:
  light_intensity: 1.0
  light_falloff: 2.0

docs.title: Ambient light
docs.text: Rays that leave the scene return the sky: the built-in gradient (background_color at the top, white at the horizon) scaled by background_intensity, or an HDR environment (HDR Sky Dome). Set background_intensity: 0 for a scene lit by its emitters alone, as in the Cornell box and the NEE scene.

docs.title: Fireflies
docs.text:
A single very bright sample, typically a path that found a small light through a specular bounce, can leave a white dot that takes thousands of samples to fade. Two mechanisms keep them in check:

  • the still image clamps each sample's luminance to a ceiling that grows with the sample count, so the estimate stays unbiased in the limit;
  • while the camera moves, isolated bright pixels are scaled down at display time (the Despeckle motion frames option), which touches the preview only;
  • the sun of an HDR sky, the brightest firefly source of all, is sampled directly by the OptiX interactive mode (sky importance sampling with MIS, see HDR Sky Dome), so it reaches diffuse surfaces through shadow rays rather than by chance;
  • what light sampling cannot reach, the indirect clamp (OptiX) holds down: a fixed per-sample ceiling on the light gathered after the first diffuse bounce.

docs.title: Indirect clamp (OptiX)
docs.text: Caustic paths, a light or the sun reaching a diffuse surface through glass or off a mirror, cannot be targeted by shadow rays. Under the growing clamp above they still converge, but slowly: the ceiling grows as \(\sqrt{N}\) and the hits arrive in proportion to \(N\), so an isolated dot keeps an amplitude of \(20/\sqrt{N}\), still visible after tens of thousands of samples. The indirect clamp is the same answer as Cycles' Clamp Indirect: everything a sample gathers after it leaves its first diffuse surface (or its first scattering event in a medium) is capped at indirect_clamp luminance per sample, 50 by default, 0 to disable. What the camera sees directly, through mirrors and glass included, and the shadow rays of that first surface are untouched, so lights, highlights and shadows keep their full value. The price is a bias on the caustics themselves: a caustic brighter than the ceiling per path (the sun focused by a glass sphere, tens of thousands per hit) is dimmed, a caustic from a lamp of emission 25 is not. The setting is per scene, live in the GUI (MIS / NEE section) and saved with the camera.

docs.title: OBJ Loading
docs.text: RayON imports triangle meshes from Wavefront .obj files and renders them with the same materials, lights and acceleration as the analytic geometry. Materials can come from the YAML scene or from the .mtl file the OBJ references, and UV-mapped image textures are sampled on the GPU.

docs.title: Supported format
docs.text:
Feature Supported Vertex positions (v) ✓ Vertex normals (vn) ✓ smooth per-vertex normals Texture coordinates (vt) ✓ UV-mapped image textures Triangular faces (f) ✓ Quad faces triangulated into two triangles Material groups (usemtl) ✓ per-group materials from the MTL MTL files (mtllib) ✓ Kd, Ke, Ni, Ns, d, illum, map_Kd

Faces with more than four vertices are not supported; export triangulated meshes.

docs.title: Loading a mesh
docs.text:
geometry:
  - type: "obj"
    material: "plastic_white"      # optional: fallback for groups without usemtl
    file: "../models/stanford-bunny.obj"
    scale: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]         # per-axis scale
    position: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]      # translation applied after scaling

The file path is resolved relative to the scene file. When the OBJ carries a mtllib, the material key may be omitted and every usemtl group uses its MTL material; a YAML material is the fallback for faces without one.

Each triangle becomes one geometry entry of the scene description, so a 250 000-triangle dragon is 250 000 entries: enable use_bvh: true for any mesh.

docs.title: MTL materials
docs.text: MTL property Effect in RayON Kd r g b Diffuse albedo Ke r g b Emission; a non-zero value makes a light material Ns exponent Converted to roughness (1 − √(Ns / 1000)) Ni ior Refractive index of glass materials d opacity Below 0.5 selects a glass material illum 0–2 Lambertian (illum 2 is the usual exporter default for a diffuse surface) illum 3 and above Rough mirror, roughness from Ns illum 5 / 7 Glass map_Kd path Image texture, resolved relative to the .mtl file

docs.title: Image textures
docs.text:
A map_Kd texture, or a texture: key on a YAML material, is decoded with stb_image and uploaded as a CUDA texture object. At a hit the UVs are interpolated with the barycentric weights of the triangle,

\[ (u, v)_\text{hit} = (1-u-v)\,(u_0,v_0) + u\,(u_1,v_1) + v\,(u_2,v_2), \]

and the texel replaces the material's albedo. Textures are loaded once and shared by path.

materials:
  - name: "textured_floor"
    type: "lambertian"
    texture: "../textures/grid_512.png"
UV mapping — a grid texture on a UV-mapped cube, sphere and ground plane (13_texture_test1.yaml). MTL-driven textures — per-group materials of a Blender export (14_texture_test2.yaml).

docs.title: Triangle intersection
docs.text:
The CUDA back-end intersects triangles with the Möller–Trumbore algorithm. For a ray \(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}\) and a triangle \((\mathbf{v}_0, \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2)\), with \(\mathbf{e}_1 = \mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_0\), \(\mathbf{e}_2 = \mathbf{v}_2 - \mathbf{v}_0\), \(\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{d} \times \mathbf{e}_2\), \(\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{o} - \mathbf{v}_0\) and \(\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{t} \times \mathbf{e}_1\):

\[ \begin{pmatrix} t \\ u \\ v \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{e}_1} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{e}_2 \\ \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{t} \\ \mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{d} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{hit} \iff u \ge 0,\; v \ge 0,\; u + v \le 1,\; t > t_\min . \]

The OptiX back-end hands every triangle to the RT cores: all triangles of the scene go into one geometry acceleration structure with the built-in intersector, and a per-triangle table holds the material, the normals, the UVs and the visible flag.

docs.title: Smooth normals
docs.text:
With vn records the shading normal is interpolated across the face, \(\hat{n} = (1 - u - v)\,\hat{n}_0 + u\,\hat{n}_1 + v\,\hat{n}_2\), which makes a low-polygon mesh look smooth. Without them the flat face normal is used.

Smooth normals — interpolated per-vertex normals on a low-poly mesh. Normal visualisation — the show_normals material (key N in the GUI).

docs.title: YAML Scene Format
docs.text: Every scene can be described in a plain YAML file and loaded without recompilation. The format is read by a small custom parser (yaml_scene_loader.cc), no external YAML library is needed. The reference below matches resources/scenes/SCENE_FORMAT.md in the repository.

docs.title: Loading a scene
docs.text:
./rayon --scene ../resources/scenes/09_color_bleed_box.yaml -s 512 -r 1080

In interactive mode the Scene combo and the Left / Right keys switch between every YAML file found in resources/scenes/. A scene loads in a few milliseconds; OBJ meshes and volume grids take longer.

docs.title: File structure
docs.text:
Four optional top-level sections, in any order. Comments start with #, values may be quoted.

camera:        # viewpoint
settings:      # render options
materials:     # named material library
geometry:      # the objects

Both materials: and geometry: entries accept the compact inline syntax:

materials:
  - { name: floor, type: lambertian, albedo: [0.15, 0.15, 0.18] }
geometry:
  - { type: sphere, material: floor, center: [0, 1, 0], radius: 0.7 }

docs.title: camera
docs.text:
Key Default Description position [0, 0, 0] Camera origin look_at [0, 0, -1] Point the camera looks at up [0, 1, 0] World up vector fov 90 Vertical field of view in degrees 
camera:
  position: [0, 2, 8]
  look_at:  [0, 0.5, 0]
  fov: 45

Save the camera from the GUI

In interactive mode, frame the view you like and press Save camera & lights to scene YAML in the Scene section. The camera: lines and the light settings of the file are rewritten in place, comments included.

docs.title: settings
docs.text: Key Default Description background_color [0.5, 0.7, 1.0] Top colour of the gradient sky (linear RGB) background_intensity 1.0 Sky brightness (GUI Ambient Light) light_intensity 1.0 Multiplier on every light's emission (GUI Lights inten.) light_falloff 2.0 Distance exponent of the lights' reach, 2 = physical (GUI Lights falloff, see Lights & Shadows) indirect_clamp 50.0 OptiX: per-sample ceiling on the light gathered after the first diffuse bounce, 0 = off (GUI Indirect clamp, see Fireflies) use_bvh false Build the BVH; recommended above ~50 objects and for any mesh adaptive_sampling true Let converged pixels stop taking samples samples_per_batch 0 Interactive batch size for this scene (0 = renderer default of 8; --samples-per-batch wins)

docs.title: Procedural patterns
docs.text:
A lambertian material can carry a pattern block: fibonacci_dots (dots on a Vogel spiral, with color, dot_count, dot_radius) or stripes (alternating bands along the sphere's local Y axis, with color).

  - name: "pokeball"
    type: "lambertian"
    albedo: [0.9, 0.1, 0.1]
    pattern:
      type: "fibonacci_dots"
      color: [0.02, 0.02, 0.02]
      dot_count: 12
      dot_radius: 0.33

docs.title: geometry
docs.text: Each entry needs a type and a material. Any entry accepts visible: false, which hides the object from camera rays while it keeps lighting the scene (and keeps appearing in reflections).

docs.title: sphere
docs.text:
- type: "sphere"
    material: "glass"
    center: [0, 1, -2]
    radius: 0.8

docs.title: rectangle
docs.text:
A quad spanned by two edge vectors from a corner. Also the usual shape of an area light.

  - type: "rectangle"
    material: "area_light"
    corner: [-1.5, 4, -1.5]
    u: [3, 0, 0]
    v: [0, 0, 3]

docs.title: triangle
docs.text: v0, v1, v2, with optional per-vertex normals n0, n1, n2 for smooth shading.

docs.title: obj
docs.text:
A Wavefront mesh, path relative to the scene file. position is applied after scale. The material key is optional when the OBJ references an MTL file. See OBJ Loading.

  - type: "obj"
    material: "silver"
    file: "../models/stanford-bunny.obj"
    position: [0, 0, 0]
    scale: [1, 1, 1]

docs.title: displaced_sphere
docs.text: A sphere with golf-ball dimples: center, radius, displacement_scale (0.2), pattern_type (0).

docs.title: sdf
docs.text:
A ray-marched signed distance primitive: shape, center, rotation (degrees, X then Y then Z) and the shape's named parameters. See SDF Shapes.

  - type: "sdf"
    material: "steel"
    shape: "death_star"
    center: [-3.5, 1.2, -4.5]
    radius: 0.8
    cutout_radius: 0.5
    cutout_distance: 1.0
    rotation: [0, 54, 0]

docs.title: Parser behaviour
docs.text:
• At most 100 materials and 1000 geometry entries per file.
  • Keys are case-sensitive. An unknown material type falls back to lambertian; an unknown geometry type is skipped with a message.
  • An OBJ that fails to load prints an error but does not abort the scene.
  • With a duplicate material name, the last entry wins.

The bundled scenes are listed in Getting Started.

docs.title: SDF Shapes
docs.text:
Besides analytic spheres, rectangles and triangles, RayON renders ten shapes defined by signed distance functions (SDFs). They are intersected by sphere tracing in the GPU kernel, on both back-ends, from one shared source file (gpu_renderers/sdf_primitives.cuh). The distance functions are Íñigo Quilez's.

18_sdf_shapes.yaml: gold mandelbulb, ceramic death star, brass cut hollow sphere, torus, glass octahedron, pyramid, capsule, box, cylinder and sphere, lit by a hidden soft box and two bulbs. OptiX, 384 spp, 720p.

docs.title: What is an SDF?
docs.text:
A signed distance function returns the distance from a point \(\mathbf{p}\) to the nearest surface of a shape, negative inside:

\[ f(\mathbf{p}) \begin{cases} < 0 & \text{inside} \\ = 0 & \text{on the surface} \\ > 0 & \text{outside} \end{cases} \]

For a sphere of radius \(r\): \(f(\mathbf{p}) = |\mathbf{p}| - r\). For a box of half extents \(\mathbf{b}\), with \(\mathbf{q} = |\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{b}\): \(f = |\max(\mathbf{q}, 0)| + \min(\max(q_x, q_y, q_z), 0)\). For a torus of radii \(R, r\): \(f = \left|\left(\sqrt{p_x^2 + p_z^2} - R,\; p_y\right)\right| - r\).

Shapes compose with unions, intersections and smooth minima, which is how the death star (a sphere minus a sphere) and the cut hollow sphere are built.

docs.title: Ray marching
docs.text:
An SDF is intersected by sphere tracing: from the ray origin, step forward by the distance the function returns, which is the largest step that cannot overshoot the surface, until the distance falls under a threshold.

t = t_enter                     # the ray is first clipped to the shape's bounding sphere
repeat up to 320 times:
    d = sdf(origin + t * dir)
    if |d| < eps(t):  hit        # eps = 1e-4 * max(1, 0.1 t): looser far from the camera
    t += d                       # or at least 2 eps once inside the band, to keep moving
    if t > t_exit:   miss

Two details matter for a path tracer, where rays also start on the shapes:

  • A hit only counts after the march has been at least 1.5 ε away from the surface once ("arming"), so a refracted ray leaving a glass octahedron is not caught by the surface it starts on.
  • The normal is the gradient of the SDF by central differences with a step of 2·10⁻⁴.

On OptiX each SDF is a custom primitive: its axis-aligned bounding box goes into the acceleration structure and __intersection__sdf runs the marcher when a ray enters the box. On CUDA the same marcher is called from intersect_geometry() through the BVH, which wraps the shape in its bounding sphere.

docs.text:
- type: "sdf"
    material: "steel"
    shape: "death_star"
    center: [-3.5, 1.2, -4.5]
    radius: 0.8
    cutout_radius: 0.5
    cutout_distance: 1.0
    rotation: [0, 54, 0]          # degrees, applied in X, Y, Z order
shape Named parameters Notes sphere radius box half_extents (vec3) torus major_radius, minor_radius Ring in the XZ plane capsule radius, height Along Y cylinder radius, height Along Y mandelbulb power (8), iterations The fractal; expensive, keep it small death_star radius, cutout_radius, cutout_distance Crater facing +X before rotation cut_hollow_sphere radius, cut_height, thickness A bowl octahedron size pyramid height Square base of side 1 at y = 0

docs.title: Materials on SDFs
docs.text: Any material works: the gallery scene puts glass on the octahedron, a clear-coat lacquer on the death star and anisotropic gold on the mandelbulb. The sdf_material type exists for the built-in demos but is not required.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: A sphere intersection is one formula; a march is 20 to 80 evaluations of the distance function, and the mandelbulb evaluates a fractal at each of them. The bounding box or sphere keeps the marcher from running on rays that miss the shape, so a few SDFs among analytic geometry cost little; a scene made of mandelbulbs is slow. The gallery scene uses settings.samples_per_batch: 2 to stay responsive in interactive mode.

docs.title: Volumes, Clouds & Smoke
docs.text:
The volume material turns a closed mesh into a participating medium: light entering it is scattered inside by a heterogeneous density field instead of bouncing off a surface. It renders cumulus clouds, smoke and fog, either shaped by procedural noise around a mesh or by a density grid converted from OpenVDB. Both GPU back-ends support it; the OptiX renderer is the one used for development.

Procedural cloud — 17_cloud_bunny.yaml: the bunny mesh, displaced by Worley and fractal noise, lit by a hidden sun. OptiX, 512 spp, 720p, 11 s. Density from data — 19_vdb_bunny.yaml: OpenVDB's bunny_cloud.vdb, the model behind the pbrt book's cloud image. OptiX, 512 spp, 720p, 40 s.

docs.title: Scene setup
docs.text:
materials:
  - name: "cloud"
    type: "volume"                 # aliases: smoke, cloud
    albedo: [0.99, 0.99, 0.99]     # single-scattering albedo: white cloud; lower = dark smoke
    density: 30.0                  # extinction per scene unit (mean free path = 1 / density)
    g: 0.5                         # Henyey-Greenstein asymmetry: 0 isotropic, > 0 forward
    noise_scale: 1.2               # frequency of the shape and interior noise
    noise_strength: 0.2            # interior modulation: 0 homogeneous, 1 full contrast
    edge: 0.05                     # depth over which the density ramps up at the surface
    lumps: 0.3                     # the noise displaces the surface by ± this many units
    billow: 0.85                   # share of inverted Worley noise: cauliflower lumps vs wisps

geometry:
  - type: "obj"                    # the mesh is only the boundary
    material: "cloud"
    file: "../models/bunny-3.obj"
    position: [0.34, -2.2, 0.02]
    scale: [2, 2, 2]
Field Default Description albedo [0.7, 0.7, 0.7] Fraction of the light scattered (vs absorbed) at each event density 2.0 Extinction coefficient per scene unit g 0.0 Phase function asymmetry; 0.3–0.7 gives the silver lining of a backlit cloud noise_scale 2.0 Features of about 1 / noise_scale units noise_strength 0.3 Interior density noise; above 1 tears holes edge 0.1 Soft edge depth; 0 = hard edge and no distance grid lumps 0.3 Surface displacement amplitude, up to 0.75 billow 0.7 0 fractal wisps, 1 rounded lumps

All of these are live in the GUI (Cloud / Smoke section): a change re-bakes the density field in a few milliseconds and restarts the accumulation.

Looks to try

density: 4 for a thin veil, 25 for a dense cloud; edge: 0 for a hard-edged fog bunny; lumps: 0.6 and billow: 1 for a torn cauliflower; g: 0.6 for a brighter rim when the sun is behind the cloud.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Shape. At load, a signed distance grid of the mesh is built on the GPU (64 cells along the longest side, brute force against every triangle). The distance tells how deep a point is inside the mesh; the surface is displaced by ±lumps along a mix of fractal and inverted Worley noise, and the density ramps up over edge units from that displaced surface. Inside, fractal noise modulates the density by noise_strength. The whole field, shape times interior, is baked into a 3D texture of 160 cells along the longest side, so the tracking loops pay one texture fetch per step instead of evaluating the noise.

Transport. The medium is traversed by delta tracking: free flights are drawn against a global majorant, each tentative collision is a real scattering event with probability density / majorant and a null collision otherwise. At a scattering event the new direction comes from the Henyey–Greenstein phase function, and a volumetric shadow ray is traced towards a light with the transmittance estimated by ratio tracking. The shadow-ray and phase-sampled contributions are combined with multiple importance sampling, exactly as for surfaces. The distance grid also gives empty-space skipping: outside the mesh, beyond the reach of the lumps, a step can jump the whole distance to the surface.

Boundary. The OptiX renderer does not trace the mesh at all: it traces a box padded by 0.75 units around it, so the lumps can bulge outside the surface. The CUDA renderer keeps the mesh as the boundary, so its lumps only carve inwards.

The complete write-up, with the design decisions and the mistakes made along the way, is in explanations/VOLUMETRIC_CLOUDS.md (in French).

docs.title: Density from data: OpenVDB and Blender
docs.text:
Instead of a mesh and noise, the material can read a dense density grid. The grid holds the whole shape; the renderer samples it straight from the 3D texture, so the light transport is unchanged. No OpenVDB dependency is needed on the C++ side: a small Python tool converts the .vdb once.

sudo apt install python3-openvdb          # OpenVDB Python bindings (Ubuntu / Debian)
curl -L -o /tmp/bunny_cloud.vdb \
  https://media.githubusercontent.com/media/AcademySoftwareFoundation/openvdb-website/master/download/models/bunny_cloud.vdb
python3 tools/vdb_to_volume.py /tmp/bunny_cloud.vdb resources/volumes/bunny_cloud.vol --cells 300
./build/rayon -m 5 --scene resources/scenes/19_vdb_bunny.yaml

bunny_cloud.vdb is 577×572×438 voxels of 0.08 units; --cells 300 box-filters it by 2 to 289×286×219 cells, 72 MB as float32. The .vol files are large and git-ignored, so each clone regenerates them (see resources/volumes/README.md).

materials:
  - name: "cloud"
    type: "volume"
    grid: "../volumes/bunny_cloud.vol"   # dense grid, path relative to the scene file
    grid_scale: 0.0656                   # scene units per grid unit: 45.8 units tall -> 3.0
    grid_position: [0.06, -1.25, -0.06]  # offset of the scaled grid
    albedo: [0.99, 0.99, 0.99]
    density: 60.0                        # extinction per scene unit where the grid reads 1
    g: -0.3

The material then needs no geometry: the loader adds the grid's bounding box as the medium boundary. The grid is normalised to [0, 1], density scales it back; edge, lumps and billow are ignored and noise_strength defaults to 0, so the GUI's noise sliders have no effect on a grid. There is no empty-space skipping for grids yet, so they render slower than the procedural volume at the same density (40 s against 11 s for 512 spp at 720p on the bunny).

docs.title: Blender smoke
docs.text:
Any Blender smoke simulation exports to OpenVDB and goes through the same tool:

  1. Select a mesh, Object > Quick Effects > Quick Smoke.
  2. On the domain: Resolution Divisions 128–256, Noise on (Upres 2). To keep the shape of the mesh, set Gas > Buoyancy Density and Heat to 0, Vorticity to 0 and the flow Behavior to Geometry.
  3. Cache: Type All, Volumes Format OpenVDB, Bake. The cache holds data/fluid_data_XXXX.vdb with the grids density, temperature and flame.
  4. python3 tools/vdb_to_volume.py fluid_data_0015.vdb resources/volumes/smoke.vol --grid density

Without a simulation, a fog volume of any mesh can be made with OpenVDB's vdb_tool (-read bunny.obj -mesh2ls voxel=0.005 -ls2fog -write bunny_fog.vdb), which is how the sample bunny was produced.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• The baked procedural field is 160 cells over about 8.5 units: at very high sample counts (around 2000 spp) the voxels of the field show at the cloud's edge.
  • One global majorant: thin regions pay many null collisions, and grids have no empty-space skipping. A coarse grid of local majorants is the planned fix.
  • No emissive media (fire), no coloured extinction, no animation. Reading NanoVDB grids directly on the GPU, and the majorant grid, are the subject of a student project described in the write-up above.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
This section covers the mathematical and algorithmic foundations of RayON's rendering pipeline. If you want to understand why the renderer produces the images it does, start here.

Ray Tracing & Path Tracing

The rendering equation, Monte Carlo estimation, the bounce loop, and why noise decreases with more samples.

Materials

Lambertian, mirrors, glass, GGX conductors, thin films, clear coat, lights and the volume material, with the math and a YAML snippet for each.

BVH Acceleration

Surface Area Heuristic tree construction, GPU iterative traversal, and 64-byte cache-line-aligned nodes.

Hemisphere Sampling

Why cosine-weighted sampling beats uniform sampling, and how the orthonormal basis maps directions to world space.

Sobol' Quasi-Random Sampling

How 128-dimensional Joe–Kuo direction vectors and Owen scrambling deliver faster convergence than pseudo-random PCG.

Multiple Importance Sampling

Next event estimation, the power heuristic, light sampling on rectangles and spheres, and how the GPU weights emitter hits.

Visual Comparisons

Four scenes with a slider: PCG vs Sobol', MIS off vs on, and both combined.

Performance Optimisations

Every optimisation applied so far, from thread-block shape to hardware triangles, with its measured impact.

docs.title: BVH Acceleration
docs.text: A Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) is a tree of bounding boxes that lets the ray tracer skip testing against most geometry in the scene. Without it, every ray tests against every object — \(O(N)\) per ray, \(O(N)\) per frame. With a BVH the average cost drops to \(O(\log N)\).

docs.title: The problem: brute-force ray testing
docs.text:
For a scene with 300 objects, a 720p render at 256 SPP fires approximately:

\[ 1\,280 \times 720 \times 256 = 235\,929\,600 \text{ rays} \]

Without a BVH, each ray tests all 300 objects: ~70 billion intersection tests. With a BVH (depth ~9), each ray tests ~20 AABB nodes: ~5 billion tests, with most early-outs. That is a 14× speedup — measured in Performance.

docs.title: Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABB)
docs.text:
Every object is wrapped in an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box — the tightest box aligned with the coordinate axes that fully encloses the object.

The AABB is defined by its minimum and maximum corners:

\[ \text{AABB} = [\mathbf{p}_\text{min},\, \mathbf{p}_\text{max}] \]

Ray-AABB intersection — the slab method:

For each axis \(i \in \{x, y, z\}\), compute the ray parameter at entry and exit of the slab:

\[ t_{i}^{\min} = \frac{p_{\min,i} - o_i}{d_i}, \quad t_{i}^{\max} = \frac{p_{\max,i} - o_i}{d_i} \]

The ray hits the box if the intersection of all three intervals is non-empty:

\[ t_{\text{enter}} = \max(t_x^{\min}, t_y^{\min}, t_z^{\min}), \quad t_{\text{exit}} = \min(t_x^{\max}, t_y^{\max}, t_z^{\max}) \] \[ \text{hit} \iff t_{\text{enter}} < t_{\text{exit}} \text{ and } t_{\text{exit}} > 0 \]

This is 6 comparisons — far cheaper than any geometry intersection test.

docs.title: Tree structure
docs.text:
The BVH is a binary tree. Each internal node stores:

  • Its own AABB (bounding both children).
  • Indices to left and right child nodes.

Each leaf node stores:

  • Its own AABB.
  • Indices of the 1–4 primitives it contains.
